items.excerpt: Despite the title, distortion isn’t the defining characteristic of walakos‘s latest. items.body: Despite the title, distortion isn’t the defining characteristic of walakos‘s latest. Much of the production is remarkably lucid, leaving enough space around the low end and harder electronic textures for small changes in timbre and rhythm to register. “Sapphire” establishes this physical vocabulary, while “Link State” opens it out, playing with depth and distance. “Recursion Error” is more nervous and insistent, its recurring rhythmic figures subtly displaced and reshaped as the track progresses. The collaborations broaden that vocabulary. “Ray” features guitar from Maksym Borovik (Maxy Force), whose pink Jazzcaster, in walakos’s own words, fills the space in the arrangement. It also gives the track a looser rhythmic character, with syncopated layers producing an elastic, slightly off-centre groove. “-RWD” reaches further into walakos’s personal history. It incorporates samples from earlier jams with his friend Mykyta Troiepольskyi (mutedbirds), a previous collaborator on “Wyciczone ptaki” from Interrupted. Old sounds resurface within a hazier, more melancholic piece, driven by a digitally treated voice that slips in and out of the surrounding texture. “1,74B COP” brings a very different voice into the album. A Colombian mother asking for news about her son serving in the Ukrainian military cuts through the electronic patterns. This creates a distancing effect giving the track an unexpected documentary weight. It is also a reminder that walakos is one half of warнякання with Anton Slepakov, a project that has produced one of the most effective ongoing chronicles of the full-scale invasion. What began as an attempt to register the war from the perspective of civilians living through it has inevitably changed as both Slepakov and walakos have since joined the Ukrainian military, shifting the project’s vantage point from life under invasion to the experience of those now serving within the war itself. The closing “Pixel (im)perfect” gathers clicks, pulses and synthetic fragments into a buoyant groove, punctuated by brief vocals and the return of the digitally treated voice heard earlier in the album. It makes for a fitting ending: busy, playful and still moving forward. Even when the music becomes melancholic or emotionally charged, baseline distortion keeps searching for movement. There is a tone of vintage in its sound but without the nostalgia. Rhythms change shape, layers thin out pulling details into focus and new variations flourish. The album is released by Dnipropop, a label that continues to function as a focal point for the city’s scene and artists orbiting beyond it. Walakos’s own note accompanying the album perhaps provides the more important context: he thanks the Ukrainian music community for continuing to make music, support one another and keep the ecosystem alive “despite all the circumstances”, dedicating his respect to those defending the country and remembering those still serving. photo by Roksolana Deineha To help us breakdown the production process of baseline distortion, I approached walakos directly. We have been in direct contact since I first interviewed him for the Ukrainian Field Notes series and it is always a pleasure and a privilige to get to speak to him. The liner notes describe baseline distortion as music written after “the familiar conditions of life had already changed”, with the title referring to a change in the basic frameworks through which you perceive the world. Musically, though, the album is very precise and rhythmically grounded, often establishing a stable groove and then altering what happens around it. What does “baseline distortion” mean to you, and did that idea influence the way you approached rhythm and structure on the record? “Baseline distortion” is a scientific term describing when an instrument’s readings begin to deviate from the norm under the influence of stimuli that are atypical for the sensor. Yes, our baseline settings have changed as well. It’s not just me, but I very often draw on my personal experience to interpret it through music. At first, one might think of constant stress, sleep deprivation, anxiety, and PTSD. But you say the tracks have become clearer and more balanced. And that, too, is baseline distortion. We all wanted a freer, more relaxed, and easier life. But times don’t let us choose. They dictate their own terms. And just like the approach to creating tracks—that’s exactly how the life of a civilian, who was supposed to become a soldier, ultimately transforms. More discipline, more clarity, more obedience. In music, this manifests in crisp grooves and adherence to a specific style. Before, I could afford to “blur” my musical vision and approach to production, but now I can’t. And I think this is an honest interpretation of my storytelling. Compared with Interrupted, there is a stronger pull towards UK club music here, but you rarely settle into a straightforward genre vocabulary. “Sapphire”, “Link State” and “Recursion Error” maintain recognisable rhythmic grids while constantly shifting accents and textures, while “Ray”, with Maksym Borovyk on guitar, opens up a much more spacious harmonic field. What drew you towards this UK-influenced rhythmic language, and how did the collaborations with Borovyk and Mykyta Troepolsky affect the direction of the album? Here, the general concept is followed. A soldier has a sphere of obedience, a sphere for interpreting orders, and personal aspects that you won’t lose no matter what. All of this is reflected in the music: there’s the “order” of the style, your interpretation of the “assigned task,” and the personal elements that keep you grounded in all of this and remain constant. Accordingly, the UK dictates the style (yes, I genuinely love and submit to it), and there’s room for interpretation through textures and accents. But all of that is just the “frame,” and there has to be a precious gem that you set into it: whether it’s a sample from a jam session with a friend that’s dear to your heart, or a melodic ambient guitar track with a shimmer from a buddy with whom you’re always joking around and almost never have a heart-to-heart. And that’s his very sincere voice. In “1,74B COP”, we suddenly hear the voice of a Colombian woman saying in Spanish that she is worried, wants to speak to her son and hasn’t heard from him for some time. Given that Colombians have travelled to fight on both the Ukrainian and Russian sides of the war, the recording introduces a disturbing ambiguity into the track. Where did you find it, who is the woman trying to contact, and what made you place this particular voice in “1,74B COP”? This is the most heart-wrenching part of the release. I’ve previously worked with this particular group of soldiers in the Ukrainian army. I have the utmost respect for these men. I’ve had deep conversations with some of them and continue to stay in touch even after they’ve been wounded or returned home. I was struck by these experienced men who led orderly, comfortable lives, who flew halfway across the globe because they couldn’t stand by and watch the injustice unfolding here. They shared my contact information with their loved ones, describing me as someone they could trust. Sometimes the mothers and wives of soldiers would call me, often in the middle of the night (since we’re in different time zones), asking about their well-being, even after I had already left my previous unit. As an empathetic person, I keenly felt the full range of emotions and struggles of a mother who, for a variety of reasons, couldn’t speak with her son. This voice is a symbolic representation of all the mothers waiting for their sons. I salute all the foreign soldiers who are helping us defend our land. As for the sample: I feel it would be unethical to use a recording of a private conversation, but I was able to convey the general meaning using modern synthesis. painting by Roksolana Deineha The album artwork depicts the painting Lost by Roksolana Deineha. What made you go for that image in particular? The painting is framed and hanging in our home. It has a very specific mood: danger, alertness, confusion, determination. I thought about the cover for quite a while; I even briefly considered going with the aesthetic of scientific instruments and their distortions. In the midst of this agonizing decision, we were talking with Roksolana — she asked me point-blank, “Describe what your album is about.” I described the moods and themes that guided me. Then she said, “Look at the wall. It seems like the guy in the painting knows what you’re talking about.” That’s when I stopped looking for another visual. You are currently serving in the Ukrainian military, while warнякання, your ongoing project with Anton Slepakov, confronts the experience of war much more explicitly through Anton’s words and your electronic compositions. baseline distortion comes out of the same changed reality but largely avoids verbal narrative. How has serving in the military affected your ability and desire to make music, and do walakos and warнякання now provide you with different ways of processing what you are living through? To be honest, war offers the living one gift amid the overwhelming horror, death, and destruction. A keener sense of life itself. Enjoying a cup of coffee, hugging a loved one, or passionately doing what you love. How does living under conditions of highly probable death affect me? In the same way. I want to drink in this life in big gulps: to greet the dawn, to see my parents, to drink coffee with friends, to create music… And yes… In warнякання, Anton’s voice truly sets the overall tone, and from that, I build music that serves as a framework and support for the stories Anton unfolds. This duo allows us to view our shared present through Anton’s eyes and highlight it. In my own project, there’s only my life, my stories, and my storytelling which shapes and determines the artistic expression of the tracks. There are plenty of stories in my life, which means there’s plenty of color for the musical canvas. I conceptualize the chosen stories, select the “musical colors,” and write the composition. That’s why even under similar circumstances the musical interpretation differs slightly. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: electronic / experimental / glitch / IDM
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑虽以失真命名，但声响整体通透，低音与电子纹理间留有充足空间，使音色和节奏的细微变化清晰可感。曲目常通过细微移位与重组塑造节奏，吉他合作带来略带错位的弹性律动，早年即兴录音的采样与经数字处理的人声交织出朦胧感。一段哥伦比亚母亲寻找在乌军中服役儿子的语音切入，赋予作品文献性重量，也呼应创作者自身从记录战争到投身军旅的语境。结尾曲以点击、脉冲和合成碎片汇成愉悦的动势。整体在怀旧质感中不沉溺于怀旧，节奏持续变形，层次不断抽离并聚焦细节，呈现动态发展的电子声响。

items.body: Kid Bucle, either knowing or unknowingly, takes a lineage built from futurism, tek-funk, broken machinery and the pleasure of the unexpected, then subjects it to contemporary pressure until something new and now begins to emerge. Contemporary electronic art: vast, physical and breathtakingly detailed Incompleteness by Kid Bucle   I have humbly decided that this extended player affords me a slightly self-indulgent opportunity to locate myself within a lineage of which I can only ever claim to be a fragment. Or at least, the Incompleteness is so good, it’s triggered a reflective expression. Regardless, here we are. By the latter half of the 1990s, the UK underground party scene had become a sprawling ecosystem of overlapping futures. We were listening and dancing to top-tier releases from Underground Resistance, Jeff Mills, Transmat, Aril Brikha, The Jedi Knights, Dave Angel and, inevitably, Aphex Twin; elsewhere tracing the Detroit lineage through artists such as Drexciya, Dopplereffekt, Stasis et al, while the years around the turn of the century brought everything from Legowelt to LA Synthesis. Ian O’Brien, and Swayzak into our mixes. Alongside all this, an apparently endless procession of mutations and crossovers moved between techno(s) and house(s)—much of which would later be flattened, retrospectively packaged and homogenized beneath the convenient umbrella of tech house. But our lived reality was considerably less tidy than the history books might suggest. Genres were still adventurous and porous. Scenes were still arguing with themselves. New sounds arrived before anyone had decided what to call them. And beneath the increasingly polished surface of the decade’s mainstream culture, something else was happening. The countercultural and artistic momentum inherited from earlier generations had not disappeared; it had dispersed. As the millennium approached—with all the absurdly romantic anxiety of a fabricated timestamp promising either technological transcendence or digital collapse—another current began to gather force. For those of us becoming desensitised to the necessary but increasingly familiar four-to-the-floor grammar of house and techno, another possibility was emerging: a renewed electro futurism that felt less like revival than reactivation. There were already telling fractures in the beat. Breakbeat had changed the landscape. Broken beat, trip hop and electronica had widened the vocabulary. And when we went out, we wanted something fast, digital, electronic and funky enough to make the body move without requiring it to march. Something that excited the central nervous system and that spoke to the parameters of our escapist fugue states. UR003 was a mainstay. “Incompleteness doesn’t feel incomplete because of any lack. It feels beautifully. incomplete because it understands that electronic music itself is unfinished—that the machine still contains possibilities not one of us has properly accessed yet.” ~Will Wonks Such electro became cool again because, for a while, it seemed to offer an escape from the routine of clubbing routines. The second generation unwittingly arrived carrying the DNA of the pioneers but operating within a newly expanded electronic landscape. Carl Finlow. Anthony Rother. Sons of Slough. Scopex Records. Tipper. Spacetime Continuum all flirted with or championed nu-skool electro. As well as a million other unsung operators, each extending and corrupting the signal. Their work reimagined the pioneering futurism of Kraftwerk alongside the electro-funk detonations of Bambaataa, Hashim‘s Al-Naafiysh, Juan Atkins‘ Cybotron and Soul Sonic Force, YMO, Thomas Dolby, Moroder, and on. The result was not a revival. It was a reprogramming: a music that understood its ancestry while refusing to remain obedient to it. And that mattered because the consequences extended far beyond electro itself. That late-90s emergence contained the seed of the genre hybridisation we now take for granted: the willingness to let one vocabulary contaminate another, to treat genre less as a boundary than a component. Twenty-five years later, the descendants are everywhere. From glitch, Vapourwave, Chiptune, and experimental sound design pursued almost for its own sake, through braindance and Drill into the innumerable hybrid forms that followed, the electronic underground has become increasingly less concerned with preserving distinctions than discovering what happens when those distinctions are deliberately ignored. Of course, in the end there are not really two seasons of electro music—before and after, old and new. There is only the thread and the evolutionary impulses across it. A single, constantly mutating continuum that survives precisely because it is repeatedly pulled apart and reassembled as we explore, as we progressively commit to a healthy artistic development, backed up against an almost cataclysmic regression as a total species. That evolutionary thread remains alive now in the work orbiting labels such as CPU, Frustrated Funk, Analogical Force, Lunar Disko, Semantica; artists such as Annie Hall, Fleck E.S.C., Plant 43, Scape One, and here, the numerous entrants within the Science Cult ecosystem—my apologies to the innumerable others omitted here in the interests of eventually getting to the point. What connects them is not simply a sound. It is a commitment to beats and textures as an ongoing unfinished technology; to the idea that electronic music can still be strange, physical, funny, brutal, sophisticated and forward-facing all at once. That it remembers its roots as we subjectively forget. Any sufficiently deep study of art eventually reveals two competing pulses within the creative whorl. One is inheritance: the necessity of what has come before, its vocabulary and accumulated possibilities. The other is departure: the impulse to misuse that vocabulary in order to discover what else it might become. Both are necessary because both ultimately serve the same purpose—to express what is, right here, right now. Then there are the anomalies. The pioneers who, for a brief period at least, appear to operate without discernible reference points; artists whose internal cosmology is so singular that influence becomes difficult to map until everybody else catches up. Aphex Twin is an obvious example for our purposes. Such figures are rare. They are timestamps rather than trends. Archetypes, if you like: creative appearances through which something enters the culture and leaves a mark durable enough to outlive its moment. It is not for me to say here whether Kid Bucle (aka Valencia, Spain-based Malsum — Ibrahim Pedernera Martinez) belongs amongst such company. Nor, really, is it the job of a review to make that kind of proclamation. No objective assessment can supersede direct subjective experience. But perhaps one purpose of this indulgent preamble is to establish the territory into which this Incompleteness release newly arrives—and to make it absolutely clear that the effort being expended here is inspired entirely by the music itself. Because finally, this is about the music. Nothing else. Incompleteness then, is a forward-facing kick in the proverbial: a prototypical experimental experience that moves in, out, around and through what we might loosely describe as electro’s most progressive potential. It does so without sounding particularly interested in protecting the borders of electro in the first place. There is a bias towards increased tempo and a natural disposition towards the collapse of genre itself—for want of a better term, post-genre. The constituent elements of electronic music are all present, but they have been liberated (obliterated?) from their traditional obligations. Tops and bottoms. Breadth and depth. Width and height. Rhythm, texture, melody and impact are scattered across the stereo field like components from several different machines forced to cooperate. The programming is scattergun, intricate and frequently exhilarating. The digi-breaks are unapologetically funkapolian. Yet beneath the technical complexity lies an innate musicality: atmosphere, timbre and cinematic texture are not decorative additions but structural components. This is music with a stank-faced sense of awe about it. One listen’s partly in admiration and partly in disbelief that someone has managed to keep so many moving parts from tearing the entire thing apart, whilst still landing in majesty and beauty. Art that hits the spot in the listener it appeared at in its creator. “Parasitos” opens the EP with precisely that tendency towards atmosphere. Broken electronic architecture stutters and strafes, evolving and mutating through vaguely Eastern folk motifs, tearing bass and binary science. Dust-and-musk textures collide with braindance-adjacent chopped Amen snares, occasionally summoning the restless imagination of early (Sony) Tipper without ever settling into anything near imitation. It is a beautifully brutal dalliance between effort and instinct, a near-perfect amalgam of technical obsession and artistic purpose. This is an electronic wonk at work inside the digital framework of contemporary electronic production—and every decision appears to have enduring consequences. “Space Feedback” is something else again. Nothing feels absent. Nothing feels superfluous. Every bolt and bough appears to have been considered, as though a bomb is being meticulously dismantled, tenderly rebuilt and then deliberately detonated anyway. It is perhaps the purest embodiment of everything this review is struggling to describe with far too many words. Broken electro structures buckle against stuttering, hard-funked woob bass; summer-warm pads provide unexpected emotional oxygen to create clean air between the mechanical clanks and insectoid impacts. The sheer finesse here is delicious. Music more than worth the cost to both composer and audience. This is, arguably, quite simply, a classic in waiting. Title track, “Incompleteness,” opens with something approaching a Villeneuve-ian majesty. Monumental synth grandeur and bubbling acid stabs occupy an immense cinematic space before the next wave of thundering rhythm begins to tenderly pound both inside and outside the implied loop. Formation and collapse coalesce in abandon. Systems establish themselves only to be interrupted by their own malfunction. It is difficult not to hear the labour in the work—not in the sense of something overworked, but because the time, technique and attention are inscribed directly into the sound. Whether innate or learned is beside the point. The skill is unapologetically on display. It is an extraordinary piece of contemporary electronic art: vast, physical and breathtakingly detailed. “Decipher” takes the closing-credits position and, true to the spirit of the EP, refuses merely to repeat what has gone before. The opportunity to say something different—to demonstrate range, shade and alternative possibility—is grasped with both hands. Thundering, rolling tribal rhythms rumble beneath high-octane strings and expansive pads, while percussive refrains and double-time synthesizer arpeggios build further cinematic dimensions around the forming rhythms. There is a wonderful sense of musicality here, almost of scoring: the feeling that the music is accompanying images we have not yet seen. And perhaps that is the achievement of Incompleteness as an apparently single release set among the routines of too many others. It understands the continuum without becoming trapped by it. Its references are not a museum of influences but raw material. The past is present only insofar as it can still be made useful. Kid Bucle, either knowing or unknowingly, takes a lineage built from futurism, tek-funk, broken machinery and the pleasure of the unexpected, then subjects it to contemporary pressure until something new and now begins to emerge. There is rare bravery in that. There is serious technique. More importantly, here there is absolute joy. The glory of art in full effect. Incompleteness doesn’t feel incomplete because of any lack. It feels beautifully. incomplete because it understands that electronic music itself is unfinished—that the machine still contains possibilities not one of us has properly accessed yet. This EP is an unequivocal 10/10 proposition. Incompleteness is available on Science Cult. [Bandcamp | Vinyl] Incompleteness by Kid BucleThe post Kid Bucle :: Incompleteness EP (Science Cult) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — There is a particular flatness to Milanese light through the cold months, an industrial grey that tends to reduce ambition to habit and every gesture to the merely reasonable. It is not, on its face, a light out of which cathedrals of sound get built from vibraphone and French horn, harp and string quartet folded into the frame of a rock band. And yet in that grey and reasonable city, at the turn between 1972 and 1973, three young musicians decided otherwise.Alberto Ravasini, Roberto Giuliani and Sandro Lorenzetti formed the first nucleus, carrying between them the vocabulary of jazz clubs and rehearsal rooms rather than concert halls. By the middle of 1973 they had doubled in size, joined by Sergio Lattuada, Maurizio Bianchini and Leonardo Schiavone, whose training had run through classical counterpoint rather than blues scales. The new sextet took the name Maxophone, a word that reads, not unreasonably, as a cousin of saxophone and megaphone, and set about proving that a band built from two opposing musical educations need not choose between them.It took until 1975 for that proof to reach record shops, by which point the golden years of Rock Progressivo Italiano, the years of Le Orme's Uomo Di Pezza and Banco's first two albums, already lay a season or two behind. Sandro Colombini, the producer behind much of Banco del Mutuo Soccorso's early success and many other credits across the decade, brought Maxophone to Produttori Associati, a label built on film scores and jazz sessions that rarely strayed into rock at all. The album was recorded across February, March and April of that year at the Ricordi studios in Milan, engineered by Gaetano Ria, and preceded into the world by a single pairing its opening and third tracks.The cover fell to Cesare Monti, working as always alongside Wanda Monti, the same hand that two years earlier had assembled the notorious collage for Museo Rosenbach's Zarathustra. Where that image courted scandal, this one is content with mystery, and the record inside asks for nothing but attention.What Maxophone built across six songs and forty minutes borrows from everywhere without settling anywhere for long. There is the choral warmth of Genesis in the vocal writing, the keyboard muscle of Emerson in Lattuada's organ runs, the wind instrument menace of King Crimson circa Lizard in Bianchini's horn and Schiavone's reeds, a jazz vocabulary that never announces itself as foreign to the material, and underneath all of it a folk undertow that keeps the whole apparatus rooted in something recognisably Italian. Harp, violin, cello and double bass arrive as guests rather than ornaments, thickening the sextet into something closer to a small orchestra without ever slowing its reflexes.- C'� Un Paese Al Mondo: a piano figure opens onto an imagined country built on ideals of fairness and unclouded truth, sung with a conviction that makes utopia sound briefly plausible, before clarinet, trumpet and a hardening guitar drag the song back toward the actual world.- Fase: the only instrumental here, and the boldest proof of what six formally trained ears can do together, guitar and saxophone trading a nervous energy that resolves, unexpectedly, into forty seconds of vibraphone stillness before the current picks back up.- Al Mancato Compleanno Di Una Farfalla: a classical guitar figure and a flute line that could have wandered in from early Jethro Tull, framing a lyric that hands a fading butterfly's colours forward to whoever comes next, tender where the album's other songs tend toward argument.- Elzeviro: church organ and a voice alone at first, then the leaden weight of the mid seventies pressing in, the image of a man outnumbered and a power already convulsing as it comes apart, before the band answers with one of the record's most searing guitar solos.- Mercanti Di Pazzie: harp and a borrowed phrase from Hindemith's sonata open onto the album's most fragile interior, a dream logic that trades argument for atmosphere and asks to be believed rather than followed.- Antiche Conclusioni Negre: horns and drums in full voice from the first bar, a nine minute survey of everything the band knows how to do, closing on a low choir over solo organ that sounds less like an ending than a valediction.An English sung version followed the same year, with new lyrics credited to a certain J. Bratel rather than straight translations, carrying different titles and a reshuffled running order. It found little of an audience abroad, and history has settled comfortably on the Italian original as the version worth defending.By 1977 the band had time for one more single, Il Fischio Del Vapore backed with Cono Di Gelato, gentler and more modest than anything on the album, and then Maxophone simply stopped. Produttori Associati's brief and uncharacteristic venture into rock had not paid off, the wider scene it belonged to was already contracting around it, and six musicians who had spent years learning to think as one orchestra went back to thinking separately. Schiavone drifted briefly through Stormy Six before settling with the pop group Accademia. All six had already lent their hands, uncredited on the album sleeve but present on tape, to Corrado Castellari's Gente Cos� that same year.It might have ended there, one record and a rumour passed between collectors, had Sergio Lattuada not spent the following decades unwilling to let it. A 2005 box set gathered the unreleased sessions under a title, From Cocoon To Butterfly, that borrowed its own imagery from a five minute song about a fading insect. Three years later Lattuada and Ravasini rebuilt the group around new players, carried it as far as a stage in Tokyo, and in 2017 released a second album carrying words the poet Roberto Roversi had written for them before his own death in 2012. The story closed for good in May of 2018, when Lattuada died and took with him the will that had kept the chrysalis open.What survives on tape from 1975 does not need that later history to justify itself, but it colours the listening all the same. Six players who might easily have spent their careers as session musicians for other people's songs chose instead to spend one album proving what happens when every instrument in the room gets a vote. The sheer plenty of ideas occasionally denies the songs the settled inevitability of the genre's very greatest single statements, and that, rather than any failure of craft or feeling, is the only real argument against calling this an unqualified masterpiece. Everything else argues the other way. Among the crowded company of Italian progressive rock's one album wonders, Maxophone stands close to the summit, and deserves to be met there. My rating: 4,5/5(Bassano del Grappa, Italy, September 2026)

items.excerpt: ミネアポリスのマックス・デヴロー。1994年生まれの彼が2026年に日本のコジマ録音からリリースしたアルバム『レジスタンス』は1本のエレキギターを用いて5つのテーマを通じて極めてノイジーで尖鋭的な響きの探究を試みている。作品はあらゆる楽器で演奏可能なオープン・ワークとして構想されており、ブックレットにはそれぞれの楽曲の図形譜が付属している。今年1月、彼が暮らすミネアポリスでD. トランプと彼が率いるICEによって引き起こされ三千人以上の逮捕者を出した大規模な非正規移民の拘束と強制送還作戦〈メトロ・サージ作戦〉の騒乱と混沌を音楽的に記録した1枚でもある。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以一把电吉他为核心，通过五个主题展开对噪音化、尖锐音色的深入探索，同时以开放作品的形式构思，任何乐器均可演奏，并附带图形谱供演绎参考。作品源自艺术家在明尼阿波利斯亲历的ICE大规模移民拘捕行动，试图用高密度、不和谐的声响记录混乱与暴力场景下的社会张力，将政治现实直接转化为声音材料。其图形谱与即兴演奏的耦合、噪音美学的系统化组织，以及对社会事件的直接回应方式，使其超越了单纯的实验声响范畴，成为带有明确时代印记的声音档案。

items.body: One has to admire the boldness of the opening of Cacciamali. It doesn’t try to dazzle; instead, it opts for understated playfulness. A faltering folk wind instrument sets the tone as if the player were testing it rather than performing on it. This is not an artist trying to impress but someone searching. Rosso Polare introduces the album as an act of exploration. The hesitant breaths soon give way to rougher growls before the music gathers momentum through the increasingly insistent drumming of Cinna Peyghamy’s tombak. “Falò” immediately shifts the atmosphere. Beginning with recordings from a bonfire, the track slowly thickens until a guitar emerges from the electroacoustic fabric, introducing one of the album’s rare melodic moments. Its simple folk-like phrase briefly offers a point of orientation before gradually dissolving back into the surrounding texture. Equally striking are the barely audible voices: “la carezza di un ricordo… il rifiuto di un ventre… il rifiuto di una madre… il rifiuto di un figlio…” (“the caress of a memory… the rejection of a womb… the rejection of a mother… the rejection of a son…”). There is no explanation and no obvious narrative. The words are uttered almost like a spell. That reluctance to foreground melody becomes one of the album’s defining characteristics. Even when recognisable instrumental gestures appear, they are never allowed to establish themselves as fixed themes. They emerge briefly before being reabsorbed into a constantly shifting ensemble in which electronics, acoustic instruments and environmental recordings occupy the same musical plane. The collaborations expand this vocabulary without disrupting its coherence. Riccardo Sinigaglia’s presence introduces a subtle dialogue between electronic abstraction and ritual memory. “Monte” overlays dense electronic textures with ritualistic drumming, children’s voices and the distant bells of grazing animals, creating a landscape that feels inhabited rather than merely observed. “Hastilude” — named after the medieval martial games derived from hasta (spear) and ludus (play) — is one of the album’s thickest sonic environments, its layers continually reshaping one another without ever settling into stable hierarchies. “1744”, created with HMOT (Stas Shärifulla), opens in an almost cinematic manner, or perhaps like the score to a contemporary dance piece, before gradually giving way to the denser electronic textures that characterise the album’s second half. The liner notes provide an illuminating framework without dictating how the music should be heard. Side A draws upon the rhythmic traditions of medieval quintain games and flag throwing, while Side B is structured around a local legend recounting a fatal duel between father and son in 1744. Yet Rosso Polare avoids illustrating either narrative. Instead, ritual and rupture become compositional principles: repetition gradually gives way to fracture, while tradition quietly coexists with loss. Equally important is the album’s treatment of place and everyday life. No location is identified, yet the accents of the spoken voices suggest northern Italy, while one overheard remark hints that the recordings were made shortly before Christmas. These details are never highlighted; they simply exist alongside the music. In “La Cruma”, snippets of perfectly intelligible conversation drift in and out of the texture without carrying any obvious symbolic meaning. They are not clues to be deciphered but reminders that this music belongs to inhabited places. Throughout the album, field recordings never function as scenic decoration. They remain part of the same sonic fabric as the instruments and electronics. That approach has characterised Rosso Polare’s work from the beginning. Whether in Lettere Animali, Bocca d’Ombra or Campo Amaro — whose “Testamento Fermo” includes an impromptu chorus formed by those present — his music has consistently embraced participation over authorship. Cacciamali is the first album released after the departure of Anna Vezzosi, yet it continues this collective ethos. Collaboration is never ornamental; it is embedded in the way the music is conceived. The title itself, Cacciamali (“chasing away evils”), inevitably recalls Ernesto de Martino’s studies of ritual and popular belief in southern Italy, particularly La terra del rimorso, alongside Diego Carpitella’s groundbreaking field recordings documenting music as a means of confronting suffering and uncertainty. Rosso Polare never quotes those traditions directly, but he seems to share an ethnomusicologist’s curiosity. His music occupies a space where free improvisation, folk memory and traces of pagan ritual coexist without hierarchy. Whistling, traditional flutes, environmental sound, electronics and percussion are granted equal importance, while the natural world and human presence continually overlap. Rather than reconstructing folklore, Cacciamali uncovers the fragile traces it leaves behind, allowing stories, landscapes and communities to emerge through listening rather than explanation. To paraphrase Alice in Wonderland, “What is the use of music with no pictures or conversations?” Cacciamali has both in sonic form. Rosso Polare photo courtesy the artist To find out more on how to chase away evils, I reached out to Rosso Polare for an interview conducted by email, after which I followed up with a couple of clarifications. One of the things I found most compelling about Cacciamali is that it never separates music from the world around it. Environmental recordings, recognisable human voices and fragments of everyday conversations continually drift in and out of the texture. They never function as documentary material, but neither do they become anonymous sound objects. Instead, they anchor the music within a living environment. How do you approach the relationship between field recordings and instrumental sound? At what point does an environmental recording stop being documentation and become part of the composition? Since the beginning of Rosso Polare, the threshold between environmental recording and tonal sound has always been some sort of challenge. In the project’s body of work, field recordings are simply treated as integral sonic material within the composition, and it’s more a matter of a mental shift: giving the same relevance to material that could generally be seen as background, and striving to put it on the same level as composed sound. On the other hand, it’s also about stepping down with regard to played music: treating it, as much as possible, as if it were a “piece of the story” rather than the highlight of the specific musician who played it. This very difficult proposition is an attempt to make these two distinct habitats coexist without one being preponderant over the other. When does an environmental recording stop being documentation? I guess it happens in a very gradual way for me, as I gather sounds with no particular structure in mind in the first place and then assemble them afterward in the studio. Though I usually tend to avoid modern human anthropophony, it’s only with the last two albums, Campo Amaro and Cacciamali, that Rosso Polare started to embrace a bit of that as well. Before that, the project leaned away from the human voice in order to make the pieces feel as “in and out of this world” as possible, I would say. On these two albums, on the other hand, there’s some sort of investigation into folklore inside me that still has something to say, I think. So yes, as I gather sounds, they start to become part of a bigger picture, but they are always treated as just sounds, in much the same way that I treat instruments. I recently spoke to Cinna Peyghamy, who described improvisation as “moderating a debate between two very different speakers.” Listening to “XIV – Pavo”, that image immediately came to mind. He brings multiphonics and an extraordinary physicality to the opening track, yet they seem to become part of a much larger sonic organism rather than taking centre stage. What attracted you to Cinna’s approach to sound, and how did the dialogue between the two of you shape the identity of the piece? I met Cinna a while back in Basel. At the time, Rosso Polare was still a duo and we were playing at Würm on the very same night as him. Stas Shärifulla, a very good friend and artist I greatly admire, had invited both acts to play, and we almost instantly connected. I really like Cinna’s quote here and find it very fitting in this conversation too. “xiv – pavo” is the opening piece of what is, for me, a very difficult album, an album about balancing both music and personal emotions, making peace with changing aspects of my life. Thematically, it started with the concept of quintain games, flag throwing specifically, as the main melodic column is made of environmental recordings from a flag-throwing game in Spoleto, which, uncommonly these days, featured horns alongside the classic drumming. Once back in the studio, I mangled these recordings into rhythmic patterns, and the horns that came with them got weird in a very interesting way: rather than resembling a specific melody, they became some sort of average fantasy of Italian folk music, not as a cliché but more out of a damaged memory, I’d say. Alongside that came what I’d describe as embracing my limitations: between starting and finishing the recording, I contracted a severe form of pneumonia, which highly affected my lung capacity and, subsequently, my ability to play wind instruments for long periods. Lots of whispers, pants, breath struggles and inhaled screams were sampled and implemented as assets to the track rather than obstacles in the process. Cinna’s drumming and modular processing added great counterpoint to the already complex patterns of the track, while also grounding the second part of the piece in a more upfront dimension of musicality. His command of the tombak is really beyond anyone I’ve had the chance to listen to, and the integration of this very tactile instrument with modular synthesis is as difficult as it gets. I felt this track was a fitting opportunity to collaborate. He received from me what was, at the time, a somewhat finished part, and the dialogue started from that. You know, how do you integrate your voice into this? What and when should you play? Stylistic questions more than technicalities, I think, ideas about the shape of the music. The role of this track as an opener was really hard to frame in the first place. The one before was an album about Italian folk traditional chants and their potential for a modern adaptation, and I still thought that thread had to be developed in some way, so that’s when the quintain came in. But, in parallel, I came across a local legend about a son dueling with his father and being fatally struck in 1744 in Lombardy, which sort of acted as a hidden subtext throughout the record, picking up this sense of loss and despair I felt while finishing the album. So “xiv – pavo“ is basically an introduction to a specific habitat for me. One aspect I found particularly interesting is that Cacciamali brings together musicians who already share artistic connections. For instance, as a curator of the Korkut Triennale, Stas Shärifulla (HMOT) invited Cinna Peyghamy to perform while Riccardo Sinigaglia comes from an entirely different generation of Italian electronic music. Rather than sounding like a collection of guest appearances, the album feels like the meeting point of several different experimental music communities. Was that network of relationships something you consciously wanted to bring together, and did those existing connections influence the way the collaborations developed? Firstly, all appearances on the record are either friends or musicians I met and shared a vision with. Stas, with his wife Julia, was part of the label (Klammklang, now inactive) that published Rosso Polare’s first album, Lettere Animali, in 2020. We’ve been friends ever since, and I was really happy to finally collaborate on something in the studio. Cinna Peyghamy, as said before, has been a staple connection since the show in Basel and resonated both in ideas and music. Riccardo Sinigaglia is the unsung hero of experimental underground music in Italy since the ’80s. I fell in love with the debut of his band, Futuro Antico, a stunning example of cosmic experimentation that went beyond Italian music at the time. We met back in 2021 at Bääfest in Milano and connected. For me, his appearance on the record is a way to continue something that happened closer to me, a sort of homage to my musical ancestry, in a way. The beauty of this scene is the possibility of bringing together communities, as you suggested: having friends representing different scenes of experimental music and making the ends meet altogether, be it on recorded media or live performances. This network is something you build along the way through true bonds and experiences. In Cacciamali, the aim was to bring together, on record, this friendship and kin built along the way. Throughout the album I had the impression that you compose less by arranging sounds than by allowing them to find relationships with one another. Even the improvised pieces display an extraordinary sense of formal control, while the more structured works never lose their spontaneity. I’m curious about your working process. When you’re developing a piece, what tells you that it has reached its final form? Is it a question of balance, density, resonance, or is there another criterion you rely on before deciding that nothing more needs to be added—or taken away? My process relies heavily on spontaneity, followed by very meticulous arranging which, as you rightly pointed out, strives to find relationships and conversation between them. I like to think of my pieces as chapters of a book or acts in a movie. Even though it’s usually not that pondered in the recording stage, I start with a few ideas. Lately, it’s more about a series of “what ifs”: “What if this melody idea goes on top of this field recording?” or “What if I record this sound in this way?” or “What if I prepare a guitar with these objects?” etc. I don’t really like to know the themes of my works at the start. At the same time, I know when I’m working on a series of tracks that will be part of a whole, and I like to think that the themes and concepts I later find words for were actually inside the sounds all along. So it’s more like extracting what I’m trying to say from the music itself. I’d say lately it’s become more common for me to have a few stories or loose thoughts in mind at the start. Then there’s a very long time that I spend rearranging and mixing, continuously questioning myself, the tracks and sounds inside, but in a properly healthy way. I’m very picky, to the point that I even annoy myself at times, so it’s a bit of a struggle. Part of me wants to get the most out of the record, but I still need to fight this race for perfection, as it’s easy to lose a fair bit of spontaneity in the music. I always want it to feel slightly rough and to retain a sense of momentum as well. When a piece has reached its final form? Fearing here that I might sound a bit trivial, but for me it’s also a matter of gut feeling. My role is to serve the music, much as a messenger serves his purpose, and I try to sense when my part is done. Usually, a piece is ready when it feels like it’s become part of the story as a whole, when it’s telling its part of the album and feels worthy of its conversation. As a follow up, since you mentioned you had pneumonia, so did you play the flute one can hear at the very beginning of the album while recovering? The flute playing at the beginning is the only flute I don’t play. I recorded it in Switzerland at the Goetheanum. On a hill, there was a man playing a sort of Buffalo Horn. I was with Stas, curiously enough. All the other flutes on the album, however, are mostly bamboo, very rough-hewn, both transverse and with traditional mouthpieces. I think there’s also a metal transverse flute at times, and a couple of recorders, of two different sizes (soprano and tenor, I think). From the pneumonia period, the wind instruments featured are mainly the simplest to play, the small ones that require less air, plus, of course, the various reworked rattles you hear. Finally, could you confirm that the voices one can hear in the track “la cruma” were recorded in Lombardy in northern Italy? Exactly, the “Cruma” recordings come from the province of Lombardy. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Chicago-based drummer and composer Gustavo Coritñas is a restless experimenter. His music often includes Latin American folk influences, sociopolitical awareness, and thrilling spontaneity. On The Drum Also Sings, Cortiñas joins forces with two other unique and stylistically very different drummers, Dave King and Isaiah Spencer, to explore the drum kit's lyricism. For instance, the three-part group improvisation, “Dialogue with the Ancestors” features a definite spirituality. Its chant-like refrains and fiery yet haunting rhythms build an exalted homage to the gods of the past and the primal world itself. Here too, the contrasting styles of the three drummers add another captivating dimension to the piece. King’s exuberant percussion with touches of whimsy, heard on the right, complements Spencer’s darkly hued thundering beats on the left. While Cortiñas, in between his bandmates, adds a contemplative, almost meditative aspect to the collective drumming. Despite the individuality of each musician, the result is delightfully cohesive, stimulating yet never jarring. The theme of transcendent mysticism runs through the entire album. On “Etinel skotol t'ixt'unel” Mayan spoken word artist Angelina Suyul recites her own poem in her ancestral tongue. A paen to the eternal and the integration of humanity within the universe, Suyul’s performance moves with the hypnotic cadence of her words. Their meaning is almost instinctively understood even before reading the Spanish and English translations. Chilean vocalist La Paula Herrera delivers Cortiñas’ song “Tu Resiliencia Es Resistencia” with emotional resonance. Her sublime artistry and eloquence amplify the hopefulness and the poignancy of the lyrics. Meanwhile, the intimacy of her voice and the fluidity of her singing enchant and mesmerize. On “Añay Pachamama” Argentinian musician Maryta de Humahuaca interprets her compatriot, María Farfán Caparros’ ode in the Quechua language. The track glorifies the natural world in a pantheistic tone. The title translates to “Gratitude Mother Earth”, and de Humahuaca imbues it with an appropriate balance of the sacred and the primal. It is simultaneously a joyous and somber religious ceremony. This conceptual framework continues with vocalist and clarinetist Anget Bat Dawid, who transforms “Psalm 23” into a powerful, impassioned plea. Her thrillingly dissonant clarinet and her bluesy shouts make this biblical verse into a life-affirming protest anthem. It also serves as the perfect conclusion for this intriguing and provocative work. On the surface, a recording made up primarily of drumming, with little other instrumentation, may sound daunting. Coritñas, however, has made it evocative enough to entrance his audience. Far from mainstream, The Drum Also Sings stirs open-minded listeners to their core. The Drum Also Sings by Gustavo Cortiñas Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 芝加哥鼓手Gustavo Cortiñas的专辑《The Drum Also Sings》以三鼓手编制为核心，联合Dave King与Isaiah Spencer探索鼓组的抒情潜能。整张专辑贯穿超越性的神秘主义主题，大量融入拉丁美洲原住民文化元素：玛雅语口头诗人以仪式化的吟诵参与即兴，智利与阿根廷声乐家用西班牙语、克丘亚语演绎大地颂歌，Anget Bat Dawid将《诗篇23》转化为充满蓝调呐喊与不和谐单簧管的抗议圣歌。三位鼓手在个性鲜明——华丽嬉戏、深沉雷鸣、内省冥想——的同时保持了整体的凝聚力。专辑以原声打击与极简配器为主，避免电声手段，却营造出足以俘获听众的氛围。这张作品同时具备学术爵士的即兴深度与世界音乐的跨文化视野，展现了非主流音乐传统与前卫创作交融的可能性。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟套装回顾了韩国作曲家兼即兴演奏家Jin Hi Kim四十年的创作生涯。从1980年代赴美研习电子音乐与作曲开始，她将韩国传统乐器玄琴（komungo）与计算机接口、信号处理技术相结合，极大扩展了这件古老乐器的声响边界。套装分为两部分：五张碟收录管弦乐与室内乐作品，四张碟记录与Gerry Hemingway、Bill Frisell等不同领域音乐家的即兴合作。作品融合韩国传统音乐根源与西方实验作曲手法，跨越图形谱、跨文化转译、即兴演奏等多种形式。艺术家在回顾中谈到年轻时与大师级即兴者合作时玄琴音色受限的挑战，以及依靠内在能量突破局限的体验。Neuma厂牌发行，呈现一位跨文化音乐家在实验音乐领域的完整轨迹。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评探讨了四张跨越十二年的即兴录音作品，聚焦于两位乐手之间的互动所产生的难以言传的第三层含义。评论者将这种集体即兴创作比作来自未知文化的赞美诗，形态可塑而意义不可穷尽。评介重点分析了Emilio Gordoa与已故Sven-Åke Johansson的二重奏专辑《Die Dritte Ebene》，其中Gordoa将两人的平行演奏描述为某种神秘幽灵般的第三维度的浮现。音乐参照Satie的家具音乐概念，以重复素材的特殊共鸣营造出恍惚、近乎出神的意识状态。Johansson与Gordoa在极简的声响材料中构建出透明而催眠的对话空间，展现即兴音乐中倾听与共情如何转化为不断变异的声景。整篇乐评语言富于哲思，强调听者在集体即兴中的主动参与与意义构建。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑融合了民谣、前卫与宗教性氛围，以中提琴、簧风琴、锤扬琴、钢琴及少量鼓、贝斯和合成器构建出朦胧而流动的声响。音乐多采用即兴方式一次性录制完成，带有近乎神秘的低语质感，仿佛穿越时间而来。主题上是对2024年末去世的父亲的纪念，开篇曲《I Am!》将诗人约翰·克莱尔的诗作配以飘逸旋律与持续嗡鸣；核心曲目《Sprigs of Heather》以中世纪圣乐般的开头转入简约的钢琴旋律；《The Final Harvest》则沉静地描绘父亲最后一次前往心爱菜园的景象。整张专辑在光与暗之间游移，难以归入单一类型，既具挑战性又饱含深情。

items.excerpt: For a 66-minute set of four-man improv, Parallels & Diagonals is a remarkably quiet record. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由四位即兴音乐人合作呈现，其中两位资深打击乐手保罗·里顿与艾迪·普雷沃斯特占据主导地位，与年轻一代萨克斯与 trumpet 乐手塞缪尔·赖特和内特·伍利的常规角色形成倒置。整张唱片长达六十六分钟，却出人意料地保持安静内敛的氛围，打击乐手通过钹的细微触感诱导出近似旋律的声响线条，而非依赖爆发性张力。两位铜管与木管乐手选择退让而非主导，让位于长者的节奏语汇，这种代际之间的权力翻转成为作品的核心结构。专辑在小厂牌 Fataka 发行，展现了欧洲自由即兴场景中跨代际对话的细腻质感，适合对实验性即兴演奏感兴趣的听众。
