items.body: For the fourth episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we head to a village room in southern Taiwan, where a group of Paiwan elders usually gather to sing their own folk songs. Into that room, one afternoon, walked a young metal drummer who had just moved home. Sauljaljui was back in Kapanan, her village in the Hengchun peninsula at Taiwan’s southern tip. Behind her were the university years, a nu-metal band, and a pile of rejected applications to Spring Scream, the festival every Taiwanese underground musician dreams of playing. She mentioned to an auntie that she still wanted to make music. The auntie said she knew somewhere… Old people’s music, she thought when the door opened onto a dozen elderly villagers with yueqin in their laps, the two-stringed Chinese moon lute, working through Paiwan songs she had never bothered to learn. She stayed anyway, pulled up a cajón, started holding the rhythm for them, and found they sang steadier for it. Soon she was playing every session, then performing with them, and they began treating her as one of their own grandchildren. It was only then, deep into that company, that she thought to ask one of the old women what she was actually singing about, and got back a memory from the woman’s childhood: a flower she’d spotted high on a cliff while playing hide-and-seek, too far up to pick, so she just stood and looked at it until the spring wind carried its scent down to her. She has said she felt ashamed and warmed at once. Folk music, it turned out, could be a way of singing the land itself, and she had been sitting in the room where it happened without hearing it. So she stopped keeping time for the elders and started learning from them, taking up the yueqin alongside the children of the village. Two strings, an instrument that had never belonged to her people, and somehow enough: she found her own idiom inside those constraints, folding in Austronesian rhythms gathered on tour and playing the lute as a rhythm section rather than a melodic voice. She sings mostly in Paiwan, a language spoken by fewer than 200,000 people and outlawed for years under colonial rule. And it was the elders, in the end, who put her on the Spring Scream stage her own band had never reached. That path led out of the village and a long way from it. Her self-produced 2025 album VAIVAIK, a title that means both searching and embarking in Paiwan, took Best Indigenous Language Album at Taiwan’s Golden Melody Awards, and its opening track “Dipin Kari Tang” took Best Arrangement. That one came out of a month she spent living and playing with musicians in Mauritius, and she recorded it with the Taiwu Ballads Troupe back home. She has worked for years inside Small Island Big Song too, which links Austronesian musicians across the Indo-Pacific around the ocean they hold in common. This October she brings all of it to WOMEX in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, another island a long way from Kapanan. Below, she talks about the elders who taught her to sing, about carrying a language most of her audience will not understand, and about what she hopes to find on the island itself. She also curates a playlist of the tracks that shaped her sound, exclusively for Rhythm Passport. You’re bringing music that moved from heavy metal in college to Paiwan melodies rooted in your home village. For a WOMEX audience meeting you for the first time, how would you introduce that journey and the sound it led to? When I moved back to my hometown from the city to work, I met an auntie. I told her that I wanted to start a band and make music, so she took me somewhere. When I opened the door, I was surprised to see that everyone inside was elderly. They were playing the yueqin and singing traditional songs. At that time, I was honestly a little confused, because to me, it sounded like boring “old people’s music.” But after I joined them, I started playing the cajón to accompany them. In fact, with the rhythm of the cajón, they were able to sing together more steadily and in sync. Eventually, I started performing with them and accompanying their songs. One experience that really stayed with me was when we were invited to perform at Spring Scream, one of Taiwan’s most well-known music festivals. It’s a festival that almost every Taiwanese underground band dreams of playing. My own band had applied to Spring Scream many times, but we were never selected. Yet after I returned to my hometown, it was my grandparents from the village who brought me onto that stage. I remember standing backstage and teaching one of the grandpas how to make the “rocker” hand gesture when he went on stage. But when he got up there, he got it wrong and shouted, “Local!” instead. And somehow, the audience went even crazier! (Laughs) One day, I became curious and asked one of the grandmas, “What are the lyrics you’re singing about?” She told me about something that happened when she was a child. One day, while she was playing hide-and-seek, she saw a flower growing high up on a cliff. She wanted to pick it, but it was too far away. So she just kept looking at that flower. When the spring wind came, its fragrance carried into her heart. At that moment, I felt a little ashamed, but also deeply warmed. I realized that folk music could be a way of singing the land itself. As I spent more time with these elders, they began treating me like their own granddaughter. Being around them also made me softer and more gentle as a person. When I sang these songs with them, I felt like I was finally hearing my own true voice. It was as if I had found myself. You’ve said hearing your grandmother sing, a memory of flowers and spring wind carried in the words, changed how you understood what music could do. Does that moment still shape what you want a WOMEX showcase, and a room of strangers, to feel? I hope that when people listen to my music, they can imagine the place where I grew up, the land, the environment, the people, and the culture that have nurtured me. I believe they can hear that my music comes from somewhere real. It carries a kind of life force that has grown directly from the land. You brought the yueqin into Paiwan music by learning it alongside children in your village, even though it isn’t a traditional instrument for your people. Will it be part of what you bring to the WOMEX stage, and what does it let you do that a purely traditional set-up wouldn’t? The yueqin helped me break through creatively. It only has two strings, so there are obviously limitations to what you can do with it. But because of those limitations, I started asking myself how I could express who I am within that restricted space. I began combining the unique melodies of my own culture with the rhythms of Austronesian cultures that I encountered while traveling around the world. Over time, that became my own way of playing. So the yueqin is not just an instrument for me. It has become an important part of my musical language, and it will also be one of the main instruments I use in my performances. VAIVAIK means searching, or embarking, and the album is really about your own journey back to your language and your roots. What do you want a WOMEX audience, most of whom won’t know that story, to understand about that search when they hear it at your showcase? My culture has given me confidence. It taught me to truly believe that “tradition can be invented.” When I became brave enough to respond to my culture with my own ideas, rather than simply following what already existed, I finally felt a sense of openness within myself. It made my soul want to see the world. And now, I want to share that energy with the world without holding anything back. You’ve spoken about your father criticising your Paiwan, and feeling empty after your first award because you didn’t fully understand your own lyrics. Carrying the language to a WOMEX audience who won’t understand a word of it either, does that history change how you’ll sing it? Creating music in my native language naturally comes with its own challenges, especially because we have experienced colonization and the loss of our culture and language. But those difficulties don’t make me feel defeated. Instead, they give me strength. It’s okay if the audience doesn’t understand my language. When I stand on stage, I believe they can still feel the conviction and energy that I carry. Sometimes I think about what the world would be like if there were no language barriers. I believe what would remain is energy. And I believe the energy that my culture has given me can cross those language barriers and allow people to feel that life force. Small Island Big Song connected you with musicians across island cultures of the Indo-Pacific around the shared subject of the ocean. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria is an island too, out in the Atlantic. Is there something about performing on another island, so far from your own, that you’re curious to explore there? I want to learn more about the history, people, culture, and environment of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. I’m also looking forward to experiencing the place beyond simply being there as a performer. I want to walk through the city, meet the people, and understand how this land lives and breathes. Your records fold Mauritian rhythms and jazz and rock in next to Paiwan tradition. In a WOMEX programme full of the world’s traditions, how do you want that mix to land, and what do you hope people take from your showcase? In the past, when I created music that involved cultural fusion, it was mostly about combining different musical styles. But “Dipin Kari Tang” was different. I lived there for a month, spending every day with local people, living together and jamming together. So this song wasn’t something I imagined from a distance. It came from a real experience and became part of me. In my culture, recognition and belonging can sometimes be more important than blood relations. If we recognize one another, then we are brothers and sisters. That’s the feeling I hope “Dipin Kari Tang” can bring to people. Even if we come from different places and different cultures, if we are willing to recognize and accept one another, we can become family. You’ve said people don’t need to remember your name, only your culture. WOMEX is built around industry attention on individual artists and their catalogues. How do you hold onto that idea in a room like that? I never imagined that one day I would step outside of myself through my music. For me, I’m really just a messenger, a person who carries and shares the things I believe in. And strangely, that gives me a sense of freedom. It’s something that exists on a spiritual level. At the same time, in the commercial world, I hope I can bring these two sides together, the spirit I believe in and my identity as a musician. I am Sauljaljui. I come from the Indigenous people of Taiwan. You wear a lot of different hats, singer, songwriter, teacher, festival organiser with KAPANAN back home. Beyond WOMEX, and maybe thanks to WOMEX, what’s next for you? This year, I bought a new van, and in September I’m going to start a van tour. I’ll be traveling to different Indigenous communities, spending about a month in each one, and sharing how my culture has guided me around the world and influenced my creative journey. I’ve been inspired by many people along the way, so now I want to walk into these communities myself and share what I’ve learned and experienced. I especially hope I can bring new ideas and courage to young people in the communities, and let them know that their culture doesn’t have to be a limitation. It can actually become the strength that allows us to go out into the world. If you could write a short, personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and find your showcase, what would you want them to know before they arrive? I’m Sauljaljui. Your long-lost half-sibling from another mother and another father. Come and listen to what I have to say   This October, Sauljaljui carries the songs of the Paiwan elders who taught her, and the two-stringed moon lute she learned beside them, onto the stage at WOMEX in Las Palmas     PLAYLIST: SAULJALJUJ X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Sauljaljui appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 排湾族音乐人Sauljaljui重返部落，从为长老们伴奏卡洪鼓到转而学习月琴，将这件非传统乐器转化为节奏声部，融入在南岛语系巡演中收集的节奏，并以排湾语演唱。其自制专辑《VAIVAIK》获金曲奖最佳原住民语专辑，融合了毛利求斯采风成果与泰武古谣传唱队的合作。乐评描述了她从金属乐队背景转向部落音乐传承的过程，以及通过Small Island Big Song串联印度-太平洋岛屿音乐的经历。作品以传统民谣为基底，但以当代节奏思维重新编织，呈现了原住民音乐的跨岛连接与现代转化。

items.body: “Cuando voy a la montaña, voy a mí“, sings Ana María Vahos on “Nuevos Horizontes”: going to the mountain is going to herself, and to a home unlike anywhere else. The mountain she names is home to Horizontes, a village of 195 people at 2,250 metres in the hills northwest of Medellín, where the houses carry their owners’ names on the front instead of street numbers. Vahos’s parents and grandparents lived there, and Sebastián Gómez Agudelo shot the video between the village and Medellín, following her through the streets and among her family. Born in San Pedro de los Milagros in 1993 and based in Medellín, Vahos writes and performs as a cantautora in a guitar-and-voice format, with the 2022 album Los Días behind her. She sings for El Búho, the recording name of Robin Perkins, who grew up in northern England, studied Latin American Studies in Glasgow, lived in Argentina and Mexico City, and started the label Shika Shika with Argentine producer Barrio Lindo in 2015. “Nuevos Horizontes” is the second single from Hogar, out 18 September on Shika Shika, an album Perkins built around field recordings of his own home life, of travel, of islands and of long evenings with friends. Hogar comes down from Latin focus, the fire in the middle of the house. The word for a home started out naming the fire it was built around. He made the record while putting down roots in France for the first time, and Vahos sings about the opposite journey: home as the place you go back to. Perkins hosts a listening party for the album on 13 September. Listen to “Nuevos Horizontes” HERE and pre-order your copy of Hogar following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: El Búho – Nuevos Horizontes Feat. Ana María Vahos appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: El Búho与哥伦比亚创作歌手Ana María Vahos合作，以Vahos家乡山区村庄Horizontes为灵感，融合田野录音与吉他弹唱。歌曲围绕“归乡”主题展开，视频穿梭于村庄与麦德林之间，呈现家庭与地域记忆。专辑《Hogar》基于制作者Perkins在法国定居期间采集的日常生活、旅行与友人聚会的环境声响，将家的概念从火焰原义延伸至归属之地。独立厂牌Shika Shika发行，拉丁美洲的乡土叙事与电子音乐制作手法相结合，在细碎的环境采样和原声吟唱之间建立温暖而私密的氛围。

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Copied from my review at my blog, "Scott's Song by Song Spotlights", where there are links for listening and purchasing.Clicking 5, but really 4.75, nearly perfect, but not quite!The artists on today's album require no introduction for most people who will be reading this. Steve Hackett & Steve Rothery have come together to create an album of instrumental music. Of course, most of you know that Steve Hackett is best known as the lead guitarist in Genesis from 1971-1977, and has had a prolific solo career since 1975, also collaborating with Steve Howe in 1986 in GTR and Chris Squire in "Squackett" in 2011-12. Steve Rothery has been the lead guitarist of Marillion on every album in their catalog plus his solo album "Ghosts of Pripyat" in 2014. Both guitarists are highly respected for their guitar skills and compositional abilities. This album is a decade in the making, with the two coming together when they could at each of their home studios and a studio called The Racket Club. The theme of the album is "the elemental power of the sea". Finally on August 28, 2026, "The Roaring Waves" will be released on InsideOut Records. Rounding out the recordings are:- Steve Hackett / guitar, harmonica- Steve Rothery / guitar, bass, keyboards- Riccardo Romano / keyboards, bass- Daniele Pomo / drums (1-5)- Leon Parr / drums (6,7)I want to thank Oliver Bergmann from Oktober Promotions, and Sharon Chevin for directing me to Oliver. As always, I receive no further compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Time to check out the music!Track 1 - The Storm (6:50)The track fades in with ocean sounds, then a mellotron string part takes over. A lead guitar melody begins, and a bolero type of rhythm begins to emerge. At 2:17 there is the sound of thunder, and a guitar riff takes the spotlight. The drums and bass are tight. This is ominous, of course, as the track depicts a storm out at sea. The guitar solo at 3:40 sounds like Rothery to my ears, but I have no indication of who is playing what. I believe Hackett took over at around 4:25; but then again, I could be wrong. The guitarists then alternate licks. This is wonderful! At around 6:00 the storm seems to come to an end and things resolve peacefully. Awesome opener!Track 2 - Sandsend (4:46)After a note that fades in, there is a calm moderate tempoed rhythm with the guitarists alternating phrases on the melody. We are in calmer, gently rocking seas now. The synth gets the spotlight briefly at 1:50. This is a nice chill-out piece of music from these guitar masters. In the last minute or so of the track, however. The musical tension seems to build up a bit. Still, it stays pretty calm. Nice track!Track 3 - Red Dragon (4:19)This has a droning, bagpipe-like quality in the intro. When the rhythm section comes in, the tempo is slightly more upbeat. I like the use of controlled feedback. One of the players has a sitar-like tone on the arpeggiated tones. I like the soundscape on this. The tempo double-times at around 2 minutes, briefly. There are a wealth of interesting tones being utilized. The focus is on the music, not the players' virtuosic abilities. Well done; an enjoyable track!Track 4 - The Roaring Waves (7:11)The title track is up next, and the name promises an exciting ride! Hackett (I assume) starts out with an impressive classical guitar bit. An ominous crescendo takes us to an orchestrated keyboard part that establishes the backdrop for the lead guitar. Not sure which one plays what, but I bet it was Steve. Obviously, both players have built a fine reputation for their abilities. The arrangement on this one is more involved than in the previous tracks. I love the crescendo at around 5:00. I like how the two are playing countermelodies at around 5:30. The classical guitar returns to close out this wonderful dynamic track. This one is my favorite, thus far. Track 5 - K-129 (7:52) According to the notes I was provided:Cinematic is right. Songs like the claustrophobic K-129, which details a submarine's final voyage to the bottom of the seabed, dark waters swirling up around it as its crew meet their doom. "You're trying to create an atmosphere", says Rothery. "I came up with the original sequenced sound, and then it's like painting a picture. You have the rhythmical and the melodic and atmospheric elements that you try and construct in such a way to take people on a journey. And it's a fascinating story. Conspiracy theorists think this Russian submarine that went missing at the end of the 60s was trying to start a war between the States and China and that the captain scuttled the ship rather than let them start World War III, incredible."The aforementioned sequence commences the track. Atmospheric guitar tones and occasional drums are peppered over the top. This one is a slow burn. Of course, there are some sonar sound effects along the way to evoke the atmosphere of a submarine. At around 4:14 a steady drum groove begins. The guitarists' lead-lines break some of the musical tension. The rhythm stops before 5:30. A new beat returns just after 6 minutes. The guitar parts are glorious! The track concludes with a single sonar tone. Terrific track. Track 6 - The Black Sea (6:41)According to the notes provided, the (actual) Black Sea is littered with the skeletons of more than 1,000 shipwrecks over the centuries. That will certainly inform the tone of this piece. It begins with a sense of foreboding. There are wonderful clean guitar tones intertwining in the first segment over a gentle 6-8 meter. A melody takes over at around 1:45. The tone of this track is very warm and melodic. There is a sense of forward motion throughout. The two play together at around 5:00 as the music reaches its climax. Afterwards, there is a peaceful resolution. File this under hauntingly beautiful. I love it!Track 7 - Pacific Coast Highway (7:31)Hackett kicks this one off with a bluesy harmonica riff that would make Huey Lewis smile. This one is a fun driving tune! There are even some wordless backing vocals. Hackett's harmonica playing is a noteworthy feature of this track, as Rothery quipped in the info sheet:"And Steve's harmonica on that is so, so good. He said to me at one point, you know, sometimes I think I should have been a harmonica player instead of (a) guitar player."There is still plenty of great guitar playing to be had, though. This one even reminds me, stylistically, of a Joe Satriani tune. This is the one where they cut loose and have some fun! And we as listeners reap the benefits! I like the syncopated riff starting around 5:15. They finally let some shredding licks loose at around 6:10. The final minute of the song has glorious choral music "aahhs". Great ending to a great album.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:I loved it! However, don't expect a proggy flurry of odd-meters and flashy solos. No, this is about the music and creating sound pictures in a cinematic way. The compositions and arrangements are top notch. The production is immaculate. If you are looking for an immersive musical experience, this is the album for you! Of course, it's fun to try to pick out which guitarist is playing what line, it's probably better to forget all of that, and let the music wash over you. I'm giving this a 4.75 out of 5 stars (95%).

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Steve Hackett与Steve Rothery两位前卫吉他大师历时十年合作完成，以海洋的自然力量为主题，呈现纯器乐的前卫摇滚作品。乐评对前三首曲目进行了逐曲解析：《The Storm》以海浪声和Mellotron弦乐铺陈，伴随雷鸣与紧凑的鼓贝斯，展现暴风雨的压迫感与最终平息；《Sandsend》节奏舒缓，两位吉他手交替演奏旋律，合成器短暂介入，营造平缓摇晃的海面氛围；《Red Dragon》则以类似风笛的持续音引入，带有受控反馈和西塔琴般的琶音质感。录音阵容包括键盘手Riccardo Romano以及两位鼓手分别负责不同曲目。整体作品在氛围营造与吉他对话之间取得平衡，体现了两位音乐家在旋律与音色上的成熟把控，属于典型的前卫吉他器乐合作项目。

items.body: Review by JavierMiranda — Datura Lodge have arrived with something that feels fully formed, confident, and genuinely exciting to listen to, the kind of record that makes you want to tell people about it.The album opens with three tracks, "Mummy", "Stone" and "98 and 94", that flow into each other without a break, and that decision alone tells you a lot about how this band thinks. It works brilliantly. By the time the suite ends you are already hooked, pulled in by the atmosphere and the melodic instinct that runs through everything they do. The arrangements are detailed and rich, with Adam Holzman on keyboards and Ben Karas adding an electrifying violin solo on "Stone", but the melodies are always front and centre, and they stick."Hole" is worth stopping on for a moment. It has that slow-build quality that the best prog tracks share, a patient emotional arc that keeps growing until the guitar solo arrives and just says everything the words could not. There is a Pink Floyd shadow over it that feels completely natural rather than imitated.And then there is "Lodge", which closes the album and is, for me, the best thing on it. It starts with a quiet acoustic passage that immediately brings Genesis to mind, not in an obvious way, just that same sense of stillness and intention. From there it builds into something bigger and more modern, but without ever losing the melodic thread. It is a really moving piece of music.I have played this album a lot and it keeps giving. One of the best progressive rock records of the year. Five stars.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the earliest Krautrock bands actually began as early as 1964 as the beat group Bentox whichwas founded by the Swiss B�eler twins, Thomas Leidenberger, and Lucky Schmidt and found themselvestouring both Asia and Germany alike however to little financial gain. By 1971 the act grew to aquintet and jumped on the burgeoning psychedelic rock scene known as Krautrock which was takingGermany by storm. With Krautrock you never really know what you're gonna get as sometimes it'sfreaky and folky and other times loud and raucous. As the newly renamed WIND, the band set sail intothe world of psychedelia adopting a plethora of sounds that included not only the kosmische soundsthat were propelled by the likes of Amon Duul II and Guru Guru but the band also looked towards theUK for inspiration drawing some of the heavy psych / early metal moments heard by the likes of UriahHeep and Deep Purple. The band's debut SEASONS showcased these styles set to a heavy psychedelic setting with not only acompetent vocalist but an organ-drenched freakout style of heavier rock with dramatic guitardistortion, fast tempos and even a drummer to keep up with it all. As much proto-metal as lysergic60s psych, WIND also focused on dreamy folk fueled passages and classical excursions making SEASONSa nice varied heady mix into a instrumentally competency seasoned with the psychedelically detached.This band from Erlangen near Nuremberg was apparently seeking a more international acceptance withlyrics in English and nice catchy melodic hooks that kept one foot in the accessible rock paradigmall the while adding the final touches of the more psychedelic Krautrock attributes that the mostadventurous trippers were dishing out in full abundance. The album features six tracks that add up to nearly 42 minutes with the final closing "RedMorningbird" just missing the 16-minute mark. While many tracks are clearly on the heavier sideincluding the opening powerhouse "What We Do Now" and the heavy as a ton of bricks "Dear LittleFriend," other tracks such as "Now It's Over" and "Romance" are more subdued and laced with soaringflute runs and acoustic guitar, touches of jazz and a completely different vibe than the heavierside of the album. The lengthy closer is perhaps the most koschmische expansive progressive piece onthe album with long instrumental drifting, dreaming meditative soundscapes and ethereal nonchalancethrough planet Lysergia although the track eventually bursts into the heavier rock. While many mayfind this album disjointed in its wild mood swings from heavy rockers on acid to well, just plainblitzed out on acid, the ease of how this cast of characters adapts from one extreme to another isactually quite brilliant and for my tastes it all offers a nice varying palette of mood settings.Sounding like Uriah Heep or Deep Purple from a parallel universe, WIND managed to emulate other actsbut really sounds fairly unique in its little in-between zone where heavy psych meets the mosttrippy expansive mediative side of Krautrock. It's actually the perfect album for 1971 which stillshowcased prog as unfinished business that hadn't quite found those formulaic approaches. WINDsuccessfully captured the heavy organ rock aspects that were en vogue at the time as well ascapturing the essence of a true psychedelic Kraut band. Perhaps the closest band i've heard toWIND's first album is another German band, Twenty Sixty Six And Then which released it's classic oneoff the very next year. Overall this is quality progressive heavy psych from 1971 Germany. The banddid release one following album but shed the rock aspects and went full on folk, a move that provedto be the band's undoing but perhaps the comparisons to Uriah Heep were too much and even thoughthis album does remind a lot of that band's earliest prog releases, it's still distinct enough standon its own two feet.
items._genre: krautrock / psychedelic rock / heavy psych / proto-metal
items._cn_summary: 这支前身诞生于1964年的德国乐队，在1971年以新名号推出首张专辑，正值Krautrock浪潮兴起。作品在重型迷幻摇滚基础上引入英国硬摇滚与早期金属的力度，同时穿插民谣、古典与爵士段落，形成强烈的情绪反差。六首曲目共约42分钟，末曲接近16分钟，以绵长的器乐铺陈和冥想式音景为主，最终仍爆发为重型摇滚。乐评指出，尽管风格跳跃剧烈，但乐队在不同极端间转换自如，整体听感既粗粝又富有变化，在同类中显得独特而耐人寻味。

items.body: Review by alainPP — Exploring Birdsong?a genre-blending act featuring Lynsey, who also provides vocals for Lifesigns, Kite Parade, Caligula's Horse, and Espera (the backing vocal group for Sleep Token)?is hailed as a reincarnation of Kate Bush. They also flirt with the style of Meer; imagine a female Einar Solberg with a touch of Leprous. Expect stunning melodies and a modern sound?prog for today that bears a slight resemblance to Kyros."Archipelago" opens with jazzy, soulful piano as Linsey's magnificent voice launches a meltingly beautiful ballad that balances delicacy and sensuality. There is a breathtaking ambient break and a dash of synth-pop?complete with strings and echoes of Meer?before the track shifts into a wild outro. "42" follows with a striking djent riff; it is heavy at its core, yet takes the form of synth-pop/electro-rock. Vocals drive this modern metal track, accompanied by siren-like backing vocals?innovative and effective. "Romanticise" leans even further into electro, featuring 80s-style synth pads that bridge the gap between mainstream pop and new wave. It carries an energetic hint of Sleep Token, building to a soaring, distorted hard-rock climax. "Footprints" is a mid-tempo ballad amplified by backing vocals and Linsey's rising vocal range. Whether segueing directly or not, "Arrhythmia" evokes a conceptual feel, characterized by a gentle tone and the lingering presence of ethereal piano and vocals. A sudden, sultry solo, a searching spoken-word passage, and a measured riff set against backing vocals enchant the space with crystalline harmonics. "Spy In The House Of Love" arrives with the solemn sound of Celtic bagpipes. It features danceable pop keyboards, an infectious groove, and a vibe reminiscent of XTC?it has it all. An 80s throwback explodes in the chorus?an addictive hook that begs to be sung along to."I_You" features subtle undertones of Coldplay; it is quintessential modern pop with a mainstream touch, yet it navigates prog territory with strings and backing vocals that recall Kate Bush. A sonic extravaganza that invites you to headbang. "The Warning" begins with the intimate folk atmosphere of Scandinavian lands; a somber melody cut through by a hard-hitting synth riff, with backing vocals amplifying the intensity. Strings heighten the drama of lyrics questioning whether to stay together or not. A vulnerable vocal performance carries a weight that flirts with decadent gothic styles. The guitars?and eventually the synths?become frenzied; simply sublime. "You Like It Best When It Hurts" follows a similar vein, bolstered by aggressive synths that evoke modern synth-prog. The riff drives forward with a heavy, rapid-fire attack that beautifully blends with ethereal keyboards. That imaginative guitar riff and the vocal harmonies are spellbinding. "Cartography" returns to the band's roots, with echoes of Kate Bush in this romantic piano ballad featuring a divine vocal performance by Lynsey. "Every House We Built" features a synth sound reminiscent of Tangerine Dream. A vocal-led crescendo builds?exploring themes of relationships and guilt?leading to an infectious drop akin to Brian Eno's work, followed by an expressive rise. "Meadowlands" is a ballad that ebbs and flows with the vocals and fresh, sparkling piano. Airy synths guide the track through a "soft-heavy" prog style, building toward a pop-infused chorus featuring the band Meer, culminating in a fiery finale before a cinematic piano outro.Exploring Birdsong delivers a thrilling fusion of pop, rock, hard synth, and progressive music worthy of Meer.(4.75)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以跨界前卫为基底，融合合成器流行、电子摇滚、民谣与金属元素。开场曲以爵士钢琴与灵魂乐人声构建抒情 ballad，随后转入氛围段落与合成器流行，再爆发为狂野尾声。作品中频繁出现重型的 djent 段落与流行旋律的对置，既有 Sleep Token 式的能量堆积，也有 Kate Bush 与 Meer 式的艺术流行气质。多首曲目引入凯尔特风笛、斯堪的纳维亚民谣、80年代合成器音色与弦乐编排，在宏大编排中保留细腻人声。专辑的写作思路并非简单拼贴，而是通过人声主导的旋律线将各类风格串联，形成兼具现代感与戏剧性的声音景观。主唱 Lynsey 的嗓音在柔和与爆发之间游走，支撑起作品的情绪张力。整体上，这是一张以旋律和氛围为核心的跨界前卫专辑，适合偏好艺术流行与重型音色交织的听众。

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 986Brand X is a British progressive rock band that was founded in London in 1975. Brand X was a jazz fusion band that was active between 1975 and 1980 and had a hiatus from 1980 to 1992. The band was disbanded in 1999 and was reformed in 2016. Brand X is one of the best, most original and well known British bands in the 70's of the jazz/rock fusion scene. Phil Collins formed Brand X in 1975, with Percy Jones, John Goodsall and Robin Lumley. The debut studio album of Brand X, "Unorthodox Behavior" that was released in 1976, presented a band more rooted in the jazz wave than in rock. From that moment, Brand X became an autonomous group, performing live with Preston Heyman on drums instead of Collins, due to his duties with Genesis, although he continued to record with them. Their second studio album, "Moroccan Roll" released in the following year, featured a fifth member, Morris Pert, in addition to Phil.So, "Moroccan Roll" is the second studio album of Brand X that was released in 1977. The line up on "Moroccan Roll" is composed by John Goodsall (backing vocals, electric and acoustic guitars, sitar and effects), Robin Lumley (backing vocals, piano, Fender Rhodes electric piano, autoharp, clavinet, Minimoog ARP Odyssey synthesizer, Roland String synthesizer and effects), Percy Jones (bass, autoharp, marimba and effects), Phil Collins (lead vocals, drums, piano and effects) and Morris Pert (percussion).With their second album, Brand X continued to develop the sound of their debut work "Unorthodox Behaviour". Many of the most familiar elements are still there, like light footed evocative jazz rock with dense textures. However, some new ingredients are also thrown into the mix. As the title itself suggests, the album features, in addition to the jazz rock mix found on their debut album, research and experiments with sounds from the Middle and Far East, mainly from countries like Morocco. So, "Moroccan Roll" delivers a competent jazz rock with small doses of oriental sounds that never make the album boring or tiring. Commercially, the band fared better with this one than with their debut, albeit to a modest extent. Overall, this is an album rated well by the critics and was very well received by the fans of the band."Sun In The Night" is a laid back music, the only one on the album that has words. It sounds neither like Morocco nor like more rock'n'roll. The intensity grows as the song progresses. This is a peculiar, but yet fascinating piece of music. The next two tracks "Why Should I Lend You Mine..." and "...Maybe I'll Lend You Mine After All" move in a completely different direction musically. "Why Should I Lend You Mine" is an excellent instrumental full of surprises ranging from its varied dynamics to the curious percussion and the always virtuous and extended sound of Jones's fretless. Lumley and Goodsall's solos move within an environment where everything seems to levitate. "Maybe I'll Lend You Mine After All" is a brief piece that could well be the coda of the previous one. "Hate Zone" and "Collapsar" complete the A side of the LP. A solo by Collins kicks "Hate Zone" for several seconds. Jones then joins in on the euphoric piece, followed by the rest of the band. This is a very hard grooving track that clearly moves towards jazz rock. The short and spacey "Collapsar" is full of various Lumley's keyboard sounds and takes us down that levitating path for a minute and a half. "Disco Suicide" is an excellent piece, one of the best built on the album. The track is divided into faster and calmer parts that sound a bit different every time they are repeated. Brand X has added vocals for the final segment of this composition. The very short "Orbits" demonstrates the instrumental mastery of Jones with his unparalleled flair and technique. The only instrument on this track is the bass and various effects. The jam session character of "Malaga Virgin" makes this track come closest to the material from "Unorthodox Behaviour". The piece switches between the fast and slow, loud and quiet parts. The interplay is exceedingly virtuosic, especially the solo segments by Jones and Lumley. "Macrocosm" is a celebration of the fusion genre, being intricate and uplifting, a showcase for the individual skills of the musicians. It shows why Brand X has been one of the jazz fusion bands with great relevance for decades.Conclusion: "Moroccan Roll", unlike its predecessor, credits the tracks to individual authors. So, obviously, it's not as jam session based as their debut album. It contains some very interesting musical ideas. The Far East sounds play a very important role. The band presents nine tracks, all of which are fascinating in their own way. From wonderfully calm songs to fascinatingly restless jazz fusion songs with progressive parts, everything is represented with the highest quality. This album ended up being the farewell of Collins, who had to leave since he accumulated the post of vocalist and drummer of Genesis. For those who want to hear developed music with emotion this record definitely offers this perfectly, but if you want the true spirit of Brand X and jazz fusion "Unorthodox Behaviour" is for sure the album to get.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items._cn_summary: Brand X第二张专辑延续首作的爵士摇滚路线，并加入摩洛哥等中东与远东声音的实验。唱片在密集织体与轻盈律动之间取得平衡，以器乐演奏为主体，融合吉他、合成器、无品贝斯和多样打击乐；曲目间的编排有动态起伏，如《Why Should I Lend You Mine》展现多变的力度与自由延展的独奏。整体上是一张把即兴能量、摇滚节奏和异域色彩结合得较为自然的前卫融合作品。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — William D. Drake's solo debut was like reshuffling the deck and starting almost from scratch, though in his case, it is a very special kind of "zero," one rich with nuances that allow for a variety of elements foreign to the Cardiacs' universe to enter the mix. It is a collection of seventeen songs, best described, were it a speech, as "logorrheic", that unfold like tales of life in nature, rural history, mysticism, mythology, and the presence of forests or the sea in English folklore (as heard in the track "The Great Adventurer"). It is no surprise, then, to find Baroque and chamber music accompanying a rock style that is highly artistic yet secular, at once cinematic, psychedelic, and dissonant. From the opening piano notes of "Miaow Miaow," we are instantly transported to another time and place; "Sky in yer Lap" feels like something out of a Shakespearean production, while "Love in an Overcoat" evokes the atmosphere of a cabaret. Throughout the album, the harmonium establishes an antique spirit, one that, in its very antiquity, becomes modern.The track "Paradox" reminded me of John Cale and his piano, evoking something visceral, raw, and stark, though Drake adds repetitive backing vocals that drive the dark, Victorian atmosphere to a fever pitch. There is something hypnotic about "Poor John"; its polyrhythms and trumpet evoke an end-of-the-world orchestra in a medieval city under siege by the plague. Yet, rest assured, "Dragonfly" pulls us away from that scene, transporting us instead to a silent movie screening."Ivy Dun" possesses a level of absurdity...of madness...that makes it one of my favorites; few pieces of music have the power to be so immediate, so direct, it strikes like an invisible bolt of lightning. That chorus and percussion, combined with the piano, don't ask for permission; they simply take hold and keep on reverberating."Lists of Clay," with its organ and deep vocals, is Peter Hammill on The Future Now; it is Gog Magog on In Camera; it is everything right in this upside-down world."Fiery Pyre," with its Eastern flair, reminded me of Siouxsie & The Banshees, while the piano and vocals could easily have been David Bowie; the album is full of nuances, secrets, and hidden compartments waiting to be discovered, each time revealing something new. It is like a labyrinth one never fully masters, despite always being in the same place.Perhaps the place itself is an illusion, a thought that arises while listening to "The Perfect Crime," a track that feels like something straight out of a 1970s Brian Eno record.And it all comes together, Cardiacs, their spirit, and an English past brought into the present with "Quivvy Vivvy." Here, a vaudeville-style format featuring multiple short songs proves the perfect vehicle to convey "Freedom and Love", fittingly, the final, deeply moving track of an ideal debut album, paving the way for several more yet to be discovered.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是William D. Drake离开Cardiacs后的个人首作，十七首歌曲如连珠炮般展开，以英国乡野传说、自然神秘主义和民间怪谈为文本，将巴洛克室内乐、歌舞杂耍与不和谐的前卫摇滚编织在一起。手风琴与钢琴营造出古旧而诡谲的维多利亚气息，时而有卡巴莱式的戏谑，时而有类似John Cale或Peter Hammill的冷峻粗粝，甚至闪现东方色彩与Brian Eno式氛围片段。多首短歌串联的杂耍结构让专辑充满跳跃感与隐秘角落，在反复聆听中不断露出新的细节。它既延续了Cardiacs的怪诞精神，又以更私密、更文学化的方式重塑了英格兰的古老回音。

items.body: In 1998, a remarkable album was released as a collaborative exchange between Sonar and Muslimgauze. Eric van Wonterghem and Dirk Ivens (Sonar) created four remixes of tracks by Bryn Jones (Muslimgauze), and the process was reciprocated. However, what wasn’t known at the time was that Bryn Jones had actually produced a total of 16 remixes, leaving it up to Eric and Dirk to decide what to do with them. Following the release, performances featuring both projects were even planned, but tragedy struck when Bryn Jones passed away in early 1999. The British project Muslimgauze was extraordinary—a project I deeply admired for its sound and its unique blend of Tribal and Middle Eastern influences. Now, so many years later, these Belgian legends have decided to release the original remixes Muslimgauze created for Sonar as a standalone album, undoubtedly driven by deep respect and admiration for Bryn Jones’s masterful body of work. The result is surprising, presenting a completely transformed Sonar sound that fits seamlessly into the Muslimgauze universe. The Belgians’ signature Power-Noise is absorbed by the force of Tribal rhythms and an Eastern atmosphere, characterized by the authentic sounds of traditional instruments. Layered on top are samples of plaintive chants and voices that further enhance the mood. Muslimgauze didn’t merely create remixes; Jones undertook a complete reconstruction of the Sonar material. The overall sound is highly minimalist and perfectly embodies the Muslimgauze aesthetic. I am also struck by the brilliant stereo effects emanating from the speakers, which lend an extra touch of distinction to the production. Through this album, Muslimgauze sounds as if the project is still alive—or perhaps newly reborn. As far as I’m concerned, this is a wonderful experience. (Rating:8). Listen to “Outtake 3”: Outtake 3 by Sonar vs Muslimgauze About Sonar Sonar is the Belgian industrial and techno side-project of Dirk Ivens, also known for his work in Klinik and Dive. The project began with Ivens working alongside Patrick Stevens (Hypnoskull); Eric Van Wonterghem (Insekt, Monolith) later joined as the group’s other core member. Sonar released its self-titled debut album in 1996, followed by “Dislocated” and “On Mission Inside” in 1997. In 1998, Sonar exchanged remixes with British artist Muslimgauze (Bryn Jones, 17 June 1961 – 14 January 1999) for the collaborative album “Sonar vs Muslimgauze”, released via Prodam Records. Jones died in January 1999, shortly after the exchange was completed. “Outtakes” gathers the remaining Muslimgauze-made remixes of Sonar material that were left unused at the time.
items._genre: industrial / tribal / dark ambient / experimental electronic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑汇集了1998年Bryn Jones为比利时计划Sonar制作的16首混音作品中的未发行部分，作为当年合作专辑的补充释出。Jones并非简单地进行混音处理，而是对Sonar原本的Power-Noise素材进行了彻底重构，将其转化为带有部落节奏与中东氛围的声音。传统乐器的真实采样与悲怆的吟唱/人声片段叠加在一起，形成极简主义美学框架下的层次感。立体声效果的处理在音箱回放时展现出鲜明特色。该专辑源于一次跨地域合作——比利时工业电子与英国部落实验声音的碰撞——在原计划共同演出之前，Jones于1999年年初去世。这份遗作的发布既是对其作品的致敬，也展现了他对他人素材进行再创作的能力，将原始素材完全融入自身美学体系。

items.body: Label: Nonesuch Records, 2026 Personnel - Henry Threadgill: alto saxophone, flute; Vijay Iyer: piano; Dafnis Prieto: drums. Henry Threadgill, a living legend, avant-garde jazz eminence, and master composer, joins forces with the incredibly creative pianist Vijay Iyer, a reference in modern creative jazz, and proficient Cuban-born drummer Dafnis Prieto, who has worked with Arturo O'Farrill, Eddie Palmieri, and John Zorn. Their debut trio album, Fifteen , comprises a strangely addictive set of post-modern and avant-garde tunes—three by both Threadgill and Iyer, and two by Prieto—that are easily recommended for fans of the three musicians. The album title refers to the number of years the trio has been performing together. Threadgill's " Trio Piece " opens the curtain in a cerebral, slow-chugging way, placing ethereal flute over mystery-inducing piano textures set in the lower register, with understated drumming punctuated by occasional syncopation. If this track gives you an idea of what comes next, " Last Night ", also composed by Threadgill, exceeds our expectations. Boasting a great vibe via its obtuse groove, the piece thrives with forward-leaning drumming, tart saxophone lines, and angular pianism. In the same feral grip of extravagance and sense of groove, Iyer's " I Wanted a Map " mixes structural rock groundwork, avant-garde literacy, and even a bit of Americana. Threadgill blows with soul on the latter, switching to flute on Prieto's " Gently Trapped ", where we can sense a classical innuendo in Iyer's playing. An ethereal flow and an agreeably smooth texture are defining characteristics of this piece. In turn, Iyer's " Fire City " goes from ruminative to ebullient, entering full explorative mode. The theme revealed at the end feels intensely bright yet typified by a few shadowy spots. Blending acute teamwork and killer textures, the trio is free to explore harmonically in the way Iyer envisioned. Yet on his pathos-packed " Perfect Victims ", he rightfully opts for simply arpeggiated sequences that further enhance its elegiac tones. In addition to wailing alto sax, we have timely cymbal washes turned thunderous tom-tom mechanics, providing a ricocheting sense of dynamism at the end. Prieto's " On the Way " packs a wallop, proving the drummer to be a skilled composer. There's a Latin freshness to it, while still bringing out Threadgill's stylistic parameters. Galvanizing percussive work, bustling piano arrays, and terse saxophone expression — all contribute to the hip swagger. This adventurous trio with a distinctly individual vibe certainly has its inventive ways of making its music sound interesting. Fifteen encompasses three strong compositional voices, leading to superior results. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Last Night ► 03 - I Wanted a Map ► 04 - Gently Trapped ► 08 - On the Way

items.album: You Us We Them :: memoryleaks (([||])) (CONDU||T)
items.excerpt: This is what it sounds like when a producer has a large collection of morning keyboard improvisations, a practice the artist calls “Chaos Works,” recorded daily as a meditative exercise, and decides to present them honestly rather than sculpting them into something more conventionally structured. A brainstorming session that stays comfortable in its own incompleteness memoryleaks (([||])) by You Us We Them   CONDUIT—stylized as CONDU||T—is a Los Angeles-based creative collective
items.body: This is what it sounds like when a producer has a large collection of morning keyboard improvisations, a practice the artist calls “Chaos Works,” recorded daily as a meditative exercise, and decides to present them honestly rather than sculpting them into something more conventionally structured. A brainstorming session that stays comfortable in its own incompleteness memoryleaks (([||])) by You Us We Them   CONDUIT—stylized as CONDU||T—is a Los Angeles-based creative collective and label operating under the ethos “how we shape the world is what the world becomes.” Since at least 2022, the collective has been releasing electronic, experimental, ambient, and downtempo music across a roster that includes Left/Right, canary yellow, Scaefa, and You Us We Them, donating a portion of proceeds from compilation releases to causes including Doctors Without Borders and hunger relief in Palestine. It’s a label with genuine community intent, and memoryleaks arrives as its most ambitious and personal release yet, a debut full-length from You Us We Them, the LA composer and visual artist whose previous work appeared scattered across CONDUIT compilation releases. 31 tracks. The first thing to establish is what to call them, not tracks in the conventional sense, but mini excerpts, ideas, fragments. Some are interludes, some are fully formed concepts, and others sound like good ideas that could have been built into something larger but weren’t. That’s not a criticism so much as an observation about intent. This is what it sounds like when a producer has a large collection of morning keyboard improvisations, a practice the artist calls “Chaos Works,” recorded daily as a meditative exercise, and decides to present them honestly rather than sculpting them into something more conventionally structured. Some of them could have expanded into larger compositions. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe they’re comfortable exactly where they sit. The melodies are the strongest element throughout and the clearest standout across all 31 pieces. The synth selection and mild effects being applied make this a beauty to listen to, bending toward ambient and experimental throughout. Comparisons to Geogaddi by Boards of Canada surface naturally, that album specifically, minus the drum work. Pure melodic bliss without rhythmic infrastructure, which leaves the melodic ideas fully exposed and either beautiful or insufficient depending on what’s underneath them. Here, what’s underneath is personal, real audio recordings collaged from childhood films, tape, and cell phone videos. A marriage proposal. Voicemails. Conversations with people no longer here. That material is embedded throughout and when it surfaces it changes the weight of everything surrounding it. Some of the darker melodic compositions and bass synth selections carry traces of Lorn‘s specific brand of dark, heavy note choices, that same gravity applied to what might otherwise float away into pure ambience. A fragment of a memory plot executed with genuine intent :: The track naming deserves attention because it rewards close reading. Usually when producers name tracks abstractly you expect the connection between title and content to be decorative rather than meaningful. Here the intent is visible. “memoryleak_non-duality”—27 seconds, is a mixture of recordings and field recordings ending with what sounds like a voicemail of a child saying “I love you.” The piece feels like someone accessing a series of memories rapidly and landing on one specific moment. The connection between title and content clicks immediately and the impact of that 27-second piece lands harder than many tracks ten times its length. “down below” applies a bouncing effect to melodies that are slowly fading and dying in sound, you can hear what sounds like seagulls or a beach setting beneath it, at least that’s what surfaces in the listening. The “memoryleak” prefixed tracks function as a distinct subcategory throughout the album, strange glimpses of something not supposed to be accessed, each one a fragment of a memory plot executed with genuine intent. A technical note worth making: a lot of the melodic structures on this album are heavily compressed. In experimental and ambient music, compression applied aggressively to melodic content does something specific, it reduces the dynamic range, bringing the quieter moments up and pushing the louder moments down until everything sits at a similar level. The effect can create a dreamlike, smeared quality where notes seem to float without natural attack and decay, which suits the memory-as-medium concept of this album perfectly. What sounds like a technical limitation is actually a compositional choice that reinforces the album’s core idea, memories don’t have natural dynamic range either. They arrive at whatever volume your mind decides, flattened or amplified by emotional association rather than actual acoustic level. “memoryleak_harbinger” is the favorite of that batch, a build that makes it feel like something epic is about to happen, then never delivers it. A woman humming, building, connecting her melodic humming to what sounds like an orchestral swell, only for it to fade and disintegrate in bitrate at the end. It is pure sound design work and a wonderful 30 seconds of listening. The album closes with “Give It Time (Life Theme)” and “rebmemeR (end is the beginning),” teasing, strange, unfinished feeling. But that’s what this album is supposed to be: an intentionally unfinished process of raw and pure melodies, a brainstorming session that stays comfortable in its own incompleteness. One thought that kept surfacing while listening: this material would make an extraordinary remix album. The melodic DNA here is strong enough that handing these fragments to other artists, from inside the CONDUIT roster or outside it, and letting them build full compositions around them feels like an obvious and genuinely exciting next step. Whether that ever happens or not, memoryleaks works exactly as it is—raw, personal, and comfortable in its own incompleteness in a way that takes real confidence to pull off. memoryleaks is a 31-track collection of short vignettes woven together with actual memories: real audio recordings from childhood films, tape recordings, and cell phone videos. His proposal to his wife, conversations with family no longer here, and voicemails from friends are all layered within. It is deeply personal. memoryleaks (([||])) is available on CONDUIT. [Bandcamp] The post You Us We Them :: memoryleaks (([||])) (CONDU||T) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: To accompany his article on Aspen Edities in The Wire 512, Peter Margasak compiles an annotated playlist of tracks from the Belgium label There’s nothing unusual about the fact that Belgian guitarist Ruben Machtelinckx started a label to release his own music. But as his Aspen Edities imprint approaches its tenth anniversary next year, the scope of the project has steadily, if quietly, expanded and changed. The label’s carefully curated catalogue has chronicled that development release by release, with almost every subsequent title carving out fresh terrain while simultaneously honouring its meditative but exploratory roots. The following playlist explores Aspen Edities’ subtly shifting outlook. Christian Wallumrød Ensemble “New hum old hum” From Non Sonett (2026) Pointing to the ECM roots of the Christian Wallumrød Ensemble is too simple. While Aspen Edities label runner Machtelinckx loves the label, the singular collision of indelible, old fashioned chamber melodies and harmonically focused expanses of sustained sound in the pianist/composer’s music feels like the stronger connection. Wallumrød continues an instinctual engagement with electronics, offering a built-on contrast when placed next to the rustic church music feel, and, as heard on the adroitly titled “New hum old hum”, explores tiptoeing gauzy timbral clouds fed through the prism of alternate tunings. Machtelinckx/Badenhorst/Cools/Gouband“Structure 6” From Porous Structures (2019) In some way the arc of the Aspen Edities’ aesthetic can be traced through Machtelinckx’s own work. This richly atmospheric quartet recording features his guitar playing clinging to vestiges of his jazz roots, with shades of Ralph Towner emanating from his interplay with fellow guitarist Bert Cools (Merope). The sui generis sound world of French drummer Tomas Gouband, who prefers to employ tree branches and stones rather than brushes and sticks on his kit, carves out a thick resonance, amplified by generous reverb, while the great Belgian artist Joachim Badenhorst toggles between liquid clarinet melodies and wordless vocals, à la Arve Henriksen. Graden/Agnas/Landin/Bromander “Chimär” From Words Were Coming Out Of Our Ears (2025) The label tapped into the Swedish scene earlier this year with this superb quartet, in which bassists Pär Ola Landen and Vilhelm Bromander actively swap and double up on roles, adding melody and fracturing time within a sub-internal dialogue. The drowsy tempos, laid out with exquisite elasticity by drummer Nils Agnas, and harmonically draped by the feather stroke touch of pianist Johan Graden, loosely evoke the legacy of fellow Scandinavian drummer Jon Christensen and pianist Bobo Stenson, but they inject a more contemporary elegant concision and directness. Dans Les Arbres “les yeux écoutent” From L’Album Vert (2024) The French-Norwegian quartet Dans Les Arbes have carved out a beguiling world of sustained tones and elusive textures on its recordings for ECM, Hubro and Sofa, but they found a simpatico landing spot for L’Album Vert, which maintains a meticulous rigour and attention to detail while embracing the fresh presence of electronic gestures and irregular rhythmic disruptions. Percussionist Ingar Zach, pedal steel guitarist Ivar Grydeland, clarinetist Xavier Charles and keyboardist Christian Wallumrød all possess extended timbral vocabularies, but they function as a single organism. Linus & BPB “Little Jesus, Mighty God” From The Outside, The Music Of Jules De Corte (2026) This new album reinforces the label’s unpredictability and breadth, as Machtelinckx’s longtime project with reedist Thomas Jillings takes a left turn into pop territory. Joined by frequent collaborator Fredrik Leroux and bassist Laurens Smet, the group interprets a selection of tunes by the once popular but now overlooked Jules de Corte, the blind Dutch singer-songwriter and pianist. Jillings translated the lyrics into English and the delicate guitar-centric arrangements make a perfect fit for the gorgeous singing of Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, who helps transform the repertoire, giving it a timeless warmth. Poor Isa “Ply” From Poor Isa + Evan Parker/Ingar Zach (2025) Machtelinckx and frequent cohort Fredrik Leroux started Poor Isa to experiment with some very unusual instrumentation: banjos and woodblocks. Through various extended techniques and the use of e-bows the project has developed a surprisingly broad soundworld, as if some bluegrass pickers were trading fours with a gagaku ensemble. A collaboration with the veteran British saxophonist Evan Parker seemed just as odd, but with the help of regular collaborator, Norwegian percussionist and sound artist Zach, they reveal a shape-shifting versatility. Oker “Crepuscular Rays” From Aerial (2026) This sublime Norwegian group entered the Aspen Edities fold through its Berlin based guitarist Fredrik Rasten, who collaborated with Machtelinckx on his hypnotising solo album Strands Of Lunar Light, a collection of serene experiments in just intonation. Oker got its start composing delicate, folk inspired compositions heavily informed by the improvisational backgrounds of percussionist Jan-Martin Gismervik, bassist Adrian Fiskum Myhr and trumpeter Torstein Lavik Larsen, but over time an attraction to spontaneity has led them to construct their pieces in real time, which Aerial captures. Still, the ensemble builds these delicate, detail-rich extended excursions with structure in mind. Veder“Sedum” From Evergreen (2017) Released in 2017, this is one of the earliest Aspen Edities titles, offering a sonic blueprint that can be connected to many of its recent releases. Machtelinckx’s calmly unfolding guitar and banjo serves as a perfect foil for the unusual braid of horns provided by Norwegian trumpeter Eivind Lønning, Belgian reedist Joachim Badenhorst, and Belgian euphonium player Niels Van Heertum, who composed these stately themes. The music is gentle but introspective, transmitting an unusual strain of chamber jazz that erases any division between extended techniques, contrapuntal elegance, and melodic generosity. Read Peter Margasak’s full Unlimited Editions column on Aspen Edities in The Wire 512. Wire subscribers can also read the article online via the digital magazine library.

items.body: An off-kilter rhythm out of West African highlife opens “Higher Levels”, and Bart Vervaeck‘s guitar threads thin microtonal lines through it that lean towards Malian desert blues, while Lieven Van Pée‘s bass bubbles beneath in a funk register. It is the second single from Collective Intelligence, the third album from Brussels quartet Echoes of Zoo, out on 2 October via Rebel Up! Records and Zephyrus Records. The quartet formed in 2018 around saxophonist and composer Nathan Daems, who also leads Ethio-jazz five-piece Black Flower. Vervaeck and drummer Falk Schrauwen play in Ghent psych-jazz collective Compro Oro, Van Pée in jazz trio De Beren Gieren. Since the 2019 EP First Provocations, through BREAKOUT in 2021 and Speech of Species in 2023, they have built a punk-edged psychedelic jazz on Middle Eastern microtonal melody and West African rhythm. Animals have set the terms for each record: BREAKOUT on the friction between humans and animals, Speech of Species on how species talk to one another, this one on how they move as a single body. The album’s second track is called “Wolf Pack Telepathy”, and Daems ties the “Higher Levels” title to the sophisticated ways animals communicate and coordinate as one, or “what we casually call telepathy, though that label says more about our own limits than what’s actually possible in nature.” Stream “Higher Levels” and pre-order Collective Intelligence HERE The post Daily Discovery: Echoes of Zoo – Higher Levels appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

Records 与 Zephyrus Records 均为欧洲小众独立厂牌，契合其地下实验美学定位。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Goh-Ka by Sigh is another great step forward for the Japanese metal legends, bringing back their earlier more manic Avant Garde black metal and thrash styles and mixing it with their recent folk, melodic and progressive metal sound. More than likely inspired by the re-recording of their classic album Hangman's Hymn, it is a return to parts of their classic sound, but not losing their recent progressive output. As always, Mirai Kawashima's manic vocals are always the unique trademark of the band, and it goes very well with the many different paths this album takes. And some of the melodic guitar work on this is very impressive. I'd give this a high 7 to low 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Kusoshi, 1 2, & 3.

items.body: Hardtack is a project founded by Frenchman Alexis Clementides. He is passionate about both technology and music, a recurring theme throughout his education and artistic career. His EP “Radiations” was released in 1999, and now, 27 years later, we have “La Dualité Originelle”, an eight-track album released via Prodam Records. Clementides immersed himself in Electro-Acoustic music, an element that is clearly audible in some of the tracks. However, there is much more to it, with the primary influence lying in what I would simply call Power-Noise. Yet the distinctive—and, to me, fascinating—aspect of his work is the fusion of Power-Noise elements with strings and other sounds that seem to emanate from the background. This gives the music a more accessible quality, creating a blend of Power-Noise and Cinematic soundscapes. It is a varied opus, featuring quieter, almost dreamlike yet abstract passages that suddenly give way to harsher, more brutal sonic onslaughts. “La Dualité Originelle” is an album that pushes boundaries and brings together diverse influences to achieve a creative and intelligent result. (Rating:8). Listen to “L’Ecole De Guerre De La Vie”: L’école de guerre de la vie by HARDTACK About Hardtack Hardtack is the project of French artist Alexis Clementides. His debut EP, “Radiations”, was released in 1999; “La Dualité Originelle” follows twenty-seven years later as his first full-length, issued on Prodam Records (Discogs). Clementides also appears on the 2020 vinyl single “Accident / Yayo88” (Deontologie) as producer. No prior Side-Line coverage of Hardtack has been found.

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”
