items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: Gerry Hemingway 领衔的国际化乐队在瑞士 Altbüron 的 Bau 4 现场录制了这张专辑，成员包括德国多乐器演奏家 Frank Gratkowski、爱尔兰钢琴家 Izumi Kimura、瑞士贝斯手 Christian Weber。作品延续了 Hemingway 在 Anthony Braxton 1985-1993 四重奏时期形成的语汇，以不对称的跳进旋律、即兴段落与谱写段落交织的结构展开叙事。36 分钟的《Bau 4 Assembly》占据主体篇幅，四位乐手齐聚，以木块等取材自木材加工厂的材料作为打击媒介，将环境元素纳入演奏。23 分钟的《Slivers》以低音单簧管与拉弓贝斯的摩擦性齐奏为骨架，铺陈自由鼓点。Hemingway 与 Kimura 的钢琴鼓二重奏片段夹在两首长曲之间，两人在共享脉动中保持即兴对话。整体呈现学院派自由爵士对长篇叙事结构与即兴张力的探索。

items.body: Steve Hauschildt recorded Nonlin when he was on tour. Representative of alienation and stark culture shocks, the sounds of LA, New York, Tbilisi, and Brussels all work their way into Hauschildt’s travel-fogged synths. Synth melodies come and go, which is indicative of a manic touring schedule where only the briefest glimpse is possible. It’s just a taste: another venue, another hotel, another flight. The nonlinear approach to Nonlin goes well with this concept of continuous, disorienting movement, the tour creating spells of chaos in its own right. Hauschildt’s city consists of melodic and dissonant architecture, and they both clash in this impressive soundscape. On the ground, strong, reassuring melodies are slowly swamped by a thick fog. In the sky, on route to another city, dense, harmonic clouds join the cumulonimbus. Predictability bends out of shape as other sequences enter the music; schedules are turned upside-down. Staccato beams of light transfix the listener, creating stuttering rhythms of their own, and other soundscapes remain beatless. There’s scope for some downtime, too. ‘Attractor B’ features a cool synth-family, but the melody meanders, and normal service is resumed with the arrival of a fast-paced and juddering beat; on the move again. The album veers between isolated pockets of rest and sudden activity. One overlaps and intrudes upon the other – not that this is a bad thing; it’s just the way it is. ‘The Nature Remaining’, for instance, is closer to ambient than it is electronica. Even though the synth-ammunition is locked and loaded, the synths settle for a slow pace, and coupled with a light reverb, the piece becomes tranquil, closing its eyes for a breather. Nonlin feels great because of these breaks, these necessary pauses, offering a smooth, frictionless motion absent of in-flight turbulence. It’s no surprise when the next track, ‘Nonlin’, presents the polar opposite, going deep into IDM and glitch-electronica. The previous track had foreshadowed it, had set it up. Even the skittering rhythm can’t hold back a radiant harmony, and Hauschildt’s variety is impressive. With nine lengthy tracks, listeners can expect the long haul, but it never feels like a laborious trek. Enjoy the ride; it’ll be over before you know it. www.ghostly.com

items.body: 1913: Adolf Loos publishes his manifesto ‘Ornament and Crime’, decrying the obvious display of labour through ornamentation as primitive and degenerate, and proposing instead the use of stripped-down, unadorned surfaces in architecture and design. 1967: In his essay ‘Art and Objecthood’ Michael Fried attacks the perceived theatricality and literalness of the emerging minimalist art movement, instead praising art that presents a single, instantaneous, timeless experience to the viewer, arguing that “presentness is grace”. 2016: Yann Novak releases “Ornamentation”, with which he critiques Loos’ aversion to race- and class-related traditions of labour and adornment through a labour-intensive, highly crafted approach to making ambient experimental music using poor-quality or technically challenging field recordings. Novak’s critique isn’t immediately obvious when listening to “Ornamentation”, mostly because the sounds themselves don’t betray any obvious manifestation of the substantial work and effort that went into creating the music. Processed field recordings are used alongside electronic chords to produce textures that vary from the heavy ephemerality of a cloud of fog rolling down a valley to the mechanical rumbling and clank of a goods train. At times, regular pulses or chord oscillations provide a strong sense of movement, while echoing clatters, clangs, and scrapes serve to situate the sounds in an urban or industrial context. Novak’s skill in balancing broad, immersive sound spectra with dynamic energy and temporal unfolding makes for an intense experience well removed from that of stereotypical ambient wallpaper. Yet the reversal of Loos’ rejection of working-class and racially-diverse traditions of ornamentation is far from clear. But take a few steps forward through the history of modernist art criticism, from Loos through Afred H. Barr and Clement Greenberg to Michael Fried, and perhaps things start to become a little clearer. By 1967, when Fried was busy defending modern art from the minimalist sculpture of Donald Judd, Robert Morris, and others, modernism had moved on from promoting the morally beneficial effects of certain types of surface finish to promoting the morally beneficial effects of a certain subjective experience of art. The kind of experience offered by truly great art, Fried argued, is one akin to a revelation: “a single infinitely brief instant,” he claimed, “would be long enough to see everything, to experience the work in all its depth and fullness, to be forever convinced by it”. This is contrasted with the time required to consider a minimalist sculpture such as Judd’s ‘Untitled 1966’, which can’t be seen all at once, but only from different incomplete perspectives. In Fried’s version of modernism, instantaneity replaces Loos’ “smooth and precious surfaces” as the mark of eternal truth and value. Novak’s work is not averse to a bit of absorbing presentness and ‘nowness’, in the sense that a piece of his music can be experienced as a single intense moment. Yet what his music resists is the claim that any such moment could offer a complete and fixed manifestation of a given thought or idea. Novak’s music is always unstable, constantly in flux, shifting from one harmonic and textural state to another, “simultaneously approaching and receding” (as Fried wrote disparagingly of theatre); it is contingent and indefinite and durational in ways that make it subtly different every time you hear it, a property that would likely horrify both Fried and Loos. What the two modernist critics were aiming for, despite their different foci, was an art that is free from the social and historical context of its production and use, transcending the changes wrought by people and their divergent worldly traditions, habits, viewpoints, and relationships. It is this ideal that Novak’s music steadfastly refutes in its embrace of multiplicity and flux. Nowhere is this refutation as clearly and as cogently expressed as on “Ornamentation”, where low-fidelity rumble and hiss connect the music palpably to a constantly changing world, and the oscillating chords, subtle pulses, and irregular incidental noises splinter the apparent unity of the moment into a thousand shards of potential.     Yann Novak Touch

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以环境音乐与实验电子为载体，对装饰与劳动的关系展开深层思辨。作者从1913年阿道夫·路斯的《装饰与犯罪》宣言出发，将视域延伸至1967年迈克尔·弗莱德对极简主义剧场性的批判，通过回溯现代主义艺术批评史的脉络，揭示劳动阶级与多元种族装饰传统被排斥的历史逻辑。制作上采用品质低劣或技术上难以处理的田野录音，与电子和弦并置处理，形成从山谷雾气般的厚重瞬态到货运列车机械轰鸣的丰富质感。规律的脉动与和弦振荡提供推进感，回声般的撞击声将听觉场景锚定于都市或工业语境。作者在宽阔沉浸的声谱与动态能量之间游走，使作品脱离背景音乐的扁平印象，同时以密集的工艺性劳动本身作为对路斯立场的反转回应。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters发行，是德国鼓手Sven Kacirek与肯尼亚传统歌手Ogoya Nengo（83岁）以及Olith Ratengo的首次三人合作。Nengo作为肯尼亚东部dodo传统的资深歌者，为作品注入了深厚的传统根基，而Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手鼓与套鼓则为声音提供了细腻的电子层。评论特别以'Bara'为例，描述了反复打击声与4/4节拍、合成低音、木琴质感逐渐浮现的过程，展现出合成复节奏与原始人声之间看似对立却最终融为一体的有机感。'Sarah'一曲中Ratengo主唱的人声与Kacirek的打击碎音形成张力，失真音效在情绪高点处适时刺入。文章将这类音乐定位为'民俗电子'谱系，与Chouk Bwa及Nyege Nyege厂牌的作品相呼应，强调其全球化语境下文化间对话却不践踏传统的特征。专辑体现场景中前卫电子与非洲传统之间相互渗透、彼此古老的张力。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)
items.label: Bongo Joe
items._genre: puxa / african rhythms / world music
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑是圣多美和普林西比70-80年代Puxa音乐的系列第二卷，由独立厂牌Bongo Joe发行。Puxa是当地独特的舞曲音乐，融合了前葡萄牙非洲殖民地的多种音乐元素，并吸收merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等加勒比与非洲节奏，形成复杂的律动织体。文章指出，尽管圣多美和普林西比是非洲第二小的国家，音乐场景规模有限，但录制的作品仍展现出旺盛的活力。专辑中的吉他相互缠绕，人声与旋律框架紧密结合，节奏部分尤其强调鼓与吉他的互动，具有强烈的舞蹈驱动力。选曲涵盖多位艺术家的现场感录音，既有紧凑的放克式律动，也有让节奏留白、突出打击乐的段落，体现了Puxa既能娱人也能通灵的双重气质。对于关注非洲音乐历史与地域融合的听众，这张合辑提供了稀缺的声音样本。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._genre: avant-garde / experimental / ambient / modern composition / art song
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是莫斯科维茨与帕拉迪诺、费拉里合作的十一首歌曲。音乐以错位、重复、忽前忽后的钢琴为骨架，叠加弦乐、木管、合成器音层与金属质感声响，刻意背离西方调性和声的惯性，接近简约主义与后极简主义的语汇。歌词兼具诗意与鲜明的现实指向，讨论威权体制如何需要自愿同谋，也直接针对方才过去的新纳粹游行，延续了六十年代抗议歌曲的传统；同时还有对死亡和人在宇宙中位置的沉思。莫斯科维茨的声音沧桑而透彻，像经验丰富的演员般赋予歌词以说服力，旋律如意识流顺词句起伏，不按预期和弦推进。钢琴时而是第二声部，时而像希腊歌队评论剧情，周围的声音框架制造脉冲与不协和。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了Antoine Dougbé与Orchestre Poly-Rythmo在1977至1982年间合作的录音。Dougbé是一位伏都教仪式音乐家，以双腿拍击的Cavacha节奏为基底，将贝宁Sato和Sakpata传统祭祀律动转化为放克形态，同时融入古巴son与刚果rumba的旋律和呼应结构。乐评特别提到录音时代的特征：合成器与带有塑料光泽的吉他交织，在密集的踩镲节奏上形成层次。例如《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》以合成器音床展开，吉他中途分散推进；《We Tayi Sin Assi Tche》则更显古巴影响，牛铃和鼻音应答贯穿。整体展现了一种根植于70年代但被时代技术重塑的声音。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: 专辑中所有乐器均由乐队成员用废品和杂物手工制作，音准与音色却出人意料地精确，在高灵敏度录音下呈现出丰富质感。音乐上融合了克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍与桑巴等多种地域节奏，并加入即兴演奏与爵士化变奏。开篇曲以欢快单簧管与低音管铺陈出犹太婚礼般的氛围，昆比亚曲目由长笛领奏并配以西班牙语合唱，标题曲则通过马林巴与非洲打击乐构建多层律动。整体上，乐队以原创自制乐器打破了传统声响边界，在民间旋律与节奏骨架中注入自由即兴精神，展现了对音乐本质的朴素回归。作品幽默而独特，既保留了世界音乐的地域色彩，又以实验性手法让这些声音焕然一新。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在意大利Fazioli钢琴音乐厅进行了一场两小时的无脚本独奏即兴录音，构成专辑《Sendas》的原始素材。后期制作中加入了人声采样、打击乐、循环音轨、田野录音和环境音效，经四十年积累的声音素材被稀疏地融入钢琴即兴之中。Sosa明确拒绝风格分类，不以爵士、拉丁或古典自居，而是将多元影响以即兴首录的方式自由组合。他在创作中追求'少即是多'的哲学，演奏不经思考、包容所谓'错误音符'，将第一遍演奏视为灵魂的自然之声。专辑在疫情封锁与婚姻结束的个人背景下诞生，被定位为精神寻路的媒介。

items.album: Synapscape releases ‘The Future’ album on Ant-Zen
items.excerpt: Synapscape, the German industrial duo of Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep, releases its new album “The Future” on 10 September 2026 through Ant-Zen. items.body: Synapscape, the German industrial duo of Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep, releases its new album “The Future” on 10 September 2026 through Ant-Zen. The 11-track record arrives on CD in a six-panel digipak and as a digital download. “The Future” mixes mechanical industrial resonance, glitch electronics and rhythm structures rooted in early EBM and downbeat minimalism, then pushes those elements through fractured textures and dark, atmospheric sound treatments. The tracklist runs “Moreish,” “Melting,” “Spring,” “Five Four,” “Dark Alliance,” “Disappear,” “Valley,” “Pick,” “To the Stars,” “Move” and “Work.” The Future by Synapscape The album is the duo’s first full-length since “Still” in 2018, continuing a catalog that Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep have built almost entirely on Ant-Zen, their home label since 1995. About Synapscape Synapscape formed in Bielefeld, Germany, in 1994, when Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep began working together on rhythmic-noise and industrial material. The duo debuted on Ant-Zen with its self-titled album in 1995 and followed it with “Rage” in 1997 and “So What” in 1999, records that paired heavy sequenced beats with noise and power-electronics textures. “Positive Pop” followed in 2001 and “Raw” in 2002, before “Act!” in 2005 and the collaborative “Scenes From a Galton’s Walk,” made with Asche, in 2006. The project continued through “Now” in 2007 and “Again” in 2009, then “Traits” in 2011 and “Rhythm Age” in 2015, moving its sound gradually from early EBM and power noise toward the more technoid, glitch-inflected direction it has kept since. “Still” appeared in 2018 as the duo’s most recent album before the current release. Münch, who also records as The Rorschach Garden and Mandelbrot, discussed his broader catalog in Side-Line’s Click Interview with The Rorschach Garden. “The Future” extends that three-decade run on Ant-Zen with its 10 September 2026 release.
items._genre: industrial / EBM / glitch / electronic
items._cn_summary: 德国工业双人组Synapscape时隔八年推出全长专辑《The Future》，延续其自1995年签约Ant-Zen以来的创作脉络。作品将机械工业共振、故障电子声响与早期EBM及低拍极简节奏相结合，再经破碎化纹理与黑暗氛围处理，形成兼具律动感与实验性的声音景观。专辑包含11首曲目，曲目名称延续了前作简短冷峻的风格，整体方向与其近年趋向技术化、微声干扰的电子路线一致。作为新闻稿，内容侧重发行信息和乐队背景，对具体声音设计的分析有限，但对熟悉该团或相关领域的听众而言，这张新作仍可视为一次风格巩固与延续。

items.body: Made your hell from the fire inside Played in flames that burned you alive What went through your head when you lost your mind The true tragedy is the world decides Something ancient in the crowd gathers around a famous death. A murder becomes spectacle; strangers study photographs, motives, wounds, and final moments as though proximity to horror might grant some secret knowledge. The macabre is easiest to enjoy when the dead are unknown to us, when grief belongs to another household and blood has no familiar name. Tragedy, then, can be consumed as theater, mystery, even entertainment. We call it curiosity, but often it is appetite dressed in respectable clothes. Civilization may depend, in part, on remembering that every spectacle was first a human life actually lived. We’ve seen it played out countless times in real life, as well as in profound films like Day of the Locust. Seattle goth dance-punk trio Holy Death Temple return with their fourth single, Nobody Loved You, a murder ballad that is shamelessly poppy and driven by a fiery bassline and fierce drumming that make the song feel almost indecently buoyant. Bryan Edward’s programming gives the track the clean immediacy of gothic synth-pop, while Jon Barrysmith’s drums keep the floor moving beneath it. Wren Rose folds guitar, synth, and backing vocals into the arrangement without crowding the hook. Edward handles lead vocals, guitar, and programming; Barrysmith (Year of the Cobra, Rifflord) takes drums; Rose (Broken Focus) supplies guitar, synth, and backing vocals. There is a little Sisters of Mercy gloom in the DNA, some Depeche Mode pop precision, and enough dance-punk velocity to place Holy Death Temple comfortably alongside ACTORS, Sextile, and VR SEX. Nobody Loved You finds its real character in the gap between what the body hears and what the lyrics are saying. The song examines the public appetite that gathers around violent death, particularly the urge to turn murder into a referendum on character. Someone dies, and almost immediately spectators begin sorting themselves into camps, prosecuting the dead, defending the killer, reconstructing motives, and deciding who deserved what. Condemnation becomes a recreational drug with excellent engagement numbers. The man at the center of the lyrics is controlling, cruel, hungry for power, and shaped by abandonment that eventually curdles into brutality. His wife endures pain and sacrifice until the arrangement ends with death. Holy Death Temple lets the listener enjoy condemning him for a while, then complicates that satisfaction by asking why everyone becomes so obsessed with determining whether a death was justified while showing far less interest in how a human being arrived at such a miserable destination. That question feels particularly sharp in an age where high-profile killings become participatory entertainment, complete with amateur detectives, moral tribunals, leaked photographs, podcast episodes, TikTok theories, and millions of strangers inspecting somebody else’s catastrophe from bed. Bryan Edward seems fully aware of how strange it is to package all of this inside something so catchy: “Never thought we’d explore our fascination with high-profile murders and repressed Erasure influence in the same song, but here we are,” he quips. “…Nobody Loved You is a mercy-killed synth-pop demo resurrected with a hook intended for a completely different track. Our best moments come from botched experiments and happy accidents.” Listen to Nobody Loved You below and order the single here. Nobody Loved You by Holy Death Temple Nobody Loved You is a bright synth-pop ‘mistake’ with a body in the trunk, built for the dance floor while staring straight at one of civilization’s uglier appetites: the thrill of death when the grief belongs to somebody else. items._cn_summary: 西雅图三人乐队Holy Death Temple带来第四首单曲《Nobody Loved You》，以哥特合成器流行与后朋克舞曲的混合架构展开这首谋杀叙事曲。贝斯线条炽热而充满推进力，鼓组在合成器下方维持舞池律动，吉他与和声层叠却不抢主唱钩子的空间。歌曲探讨公众对暴力的消费欲——目击者如何将死亡转化为道德审判与娱乐素材，受害者的完整人生却被遗忘在舆论之外。歌词描绘一位因被遗弃而走向残忍的权力欲男子，最终以悲剧收场。乐评指出作品借鉴了Sisters of Mercy的阴郁气质与Depeche Mode的流行精度，同时拥有足够的舞曲能量可与ACTORS、Sextile并置。整体在主题深度与听觉张力之间取得了较好的平衡，但旋律层面的流行化取向略显传统。

items.body: Hands in the sky and then we die Our hearts have joined the thousand We take a step into the night Opening our eyes brings a new dawn The Goth subculture has survived for nearly half a century partly because every few years somebody remembers that death can be absurd. Strip away that humour and the genre starts resembling a homeowners’ association for people with excellent boots: approved haircuts, approved records, approved photographs taken beside approved statues in approved cemeteries. Then Comes Silence have enough mileage behind them to recognize the danger. Remaker Redeemer finds the Stockholm trio Alex Svenson, Jonas Fransson, and Hugo Zombie treating the graveyard as a playground again. Then Comes Silence fortunately remembers that a black shirt is still a shirt. The album itself is conceived as a diptych, with “Requiem” representing darkness and “Ballroom” representing light. “Everything exists in contrast,” the band says. Remaker Redeemer introduces the “Ballroom” half of the band’s forthcoming Requiem Ballroom, due November 20. The band explains that the song “is about new life, being reborn with old sins washed away. A kind of cleansing, a fresh start, and the feeling of beginning again. The choice of instruments and sounds on this track was also a way to explore something a bit different this time.” Svenson’s bass plants every movement firmly beneath the feet, while Fransson’s drums drive the song with a dark, danceable force reminiscent of Killing Joke’s Night Time era. Svenson’s grave, commanding vocals strengthen the comparison, while Zombie’s guitar cuts through with a bright, sharp edge. There is genuine pleasure in the performance, closer to liberation than solemn contemplation, which suits a song concerned with starting over. Rebirth here apparently requires amplification, eyeliner, and several people dressed as failed medical experiments. The song’s lyrics treat death as a passage toward renewal, moving from surrender and darkness toward another existence. Closed eyes, raised hands, joined hearts, and the arrival of dawn suggest a collective transformation, while the repeated call to a remaker and redeemer turns rebirth into an act of cleansing: old sins washed away, one life surrendered, and another beginning on the other side. The video makes the album’s concept pleasantly mischievous. Renewal takes place among monsters. Cleansing occurs in a room full of freaks. Life returns while death watches from the front row. Directed by Damon Zurawski of Future Legends Films, the video places the band before a congregation of ghouls, Droogs, demons, grotesques, and evil babies. Yes, evil babies that look like escapees from the bargain bin of some forbidden 1970s horror shop, which immediately gives the clip more personality than another five minutes of serious men staring into industrial fog. Zurawski photographs the performance beautifully while allowing the absurdity to breathe. Svenson holds court on bass and vocals with severe composure while Fransson hammers away behind him and Zombie sends guitar across the room in sharp strokes. Around them, the assembled creatures stare, convulse, leer, and generally behave like the clientele of a nightclub whose liquor license was issued by Satan. Watch the video for Remaker Redeemer below: Rock music periodically develops the delusion that dignity equals importance, an especially fatal mistake for any subculture born from makeup, theatrical clothing, cheap smoke machines, horror films, and teenagers trying to scandalize their parents. The original punk impulse understood spectacle as provocation. Somewhere along the road, certain corners of underground culture began treating their uniforms with the solemnity of military dress. That final joke may be the best one. Subcultures survive through mutation, bad taste, risk, exaggeration, and people willing to make fools of themselves in public. Then Comes Silence understands that preservation without mischief eventually becomes embalming. Remaker Redeemer puts the corpse back on its feet, gives it a bass guitar, and lets the evil babies dance. Then Comes Silence are currently on tour in mainland Europe. items.body: Punk may have changed the musical landscape and proved that anyone with a guitar and a mission statement could start a band, but the years that followed expanded punk’s simplicity in countless exciting directions. Sometimes, it blows my mind just how many incredible bands and movements formed in the wake of the punk explosion. From 1976-1982 alone, the sheer amount of musical creativity is staggering, with so many bands quick to combine punk’s feral, DIY essence with art rock instrumentation; spacier, dubbed-out rhythms; bleak industrial textures; and much, much more. In the UK, hundreds of bands formed in the wake of the Sex Pistols, who begat Joy Division, The Banshees, and Cabaret Voltaire, who begat thousands of other bands that we all know and love today. One of the most lasting and beloved bands from the original UK post-punk boom was Sad Lovers & Giants. Formed in Watford in 1980 by Garce (Simon) Allard, guitarist Simon Blanchard, bassist Cliff Silver, drummer Nigel Pollard, and keyboardist/saxophonist David Wood, Sad Lovers & Giants (SLAG for short), quickly signed with Last Movement and Midnight Music and released a string of crucial early singles as a statement of intent. During those early years, the band was extremely prolific, cutting two moody full-length LPs in addition to these singles, each track as powerful as the last. The band caught the ear of John Peel and cultivated a devout cult following both on the strength of their studio recordings as well as their explosive live show. Soon after, the band would splinter, with Blanchard and Powell leaving to form The Snake Corps. In 1987, SLAG would reform with a new lineup and release three incredible records that saw the band expanding their sound and influencing the budding dream pop movement. 1987’s The Mirror Test is a landmark album for me personally, and it’s impressive to hear the album’s lush textures reflected in countless bands today. Again, in 1991, the band went on hiatus, but have since returned in the new millennium and have rekindled the spark that brought them together all those years ago. Since reuniting in 2002 (and again in 2009 with Pollard), the band has performed hundreds of gigs (including their first series of shows in North America in 2016), recorded a session for LA’s Part Time Punks, released a handful of standalone singles, and recorded two full-length LPs. Their latest release, this year’s The Weight of Forgotten Dreams, features ten new tracks, all of which stay true to SLAG’s majestic sound and atmospheric energy. The album is currently available on CD, digital, and vinyl, and will be followed up by a highly anticipated documentary that aims to capture the band’s many evolutions and highlights over their 40+ year career. We had the chance to catch up with the current incarnation of SLAG, including vocalist/guitarist Garce Allard, original drummer Nigel Pollard, and current members Tony McGuinness, Will Hicks, and Ian Gibson, about the new album, the band’s legacy, and more. Former guitarist and close friend Simon Blanchard also drops in for a spell… Congratulations on the new album! Can you tell us a bit about the recording of it? Garce: Our writing and recording processes aren’t separate. We have home studios in which we produce demos that are saved into a SLAG Dropbox, there are files for demos, instrumentals and raw vocal and sax stems. If anyone comes up with a demo it goes in the appropriate file. I always save a AIFF of my raw vocals at every stage. Usually what happens next is that the demos are played at rehearsal and everybody contributes ideas. Quite often these ideas are road tested at live shows and subtle changes are made, then it’s back to the original demo which gets an upgrade. When the demo file and instrumental file look like they are full enough to consider an album we produce a provisional running order and work out what needs doing to each track before it can be handed over to Igor and Tony to mix. Effectively, all the recording is done at home. The only time we go into a recording studio is if I need to ‘perform’ my vocals as we often notice they are different when I sing them in front of other people. This didn’t happen with the new record, so every vocal was recorded in the studio at the bottom of my garden. On a personal note, I write all the lyrics and whilst the others freely critique them I mainly use Nigel as a specific sounding board while a song develops, but Tony ultimately produces my vocals from the raw stems that I have comp’d and uploaded to the Dropbox file. Tony is the only person on the planet I would trust to edit the actual words I write as happened with a song on The Weight of Forgotten Dreams where I just got lost in thickets of words which needed a sympathetic pruning! Very occasionally we look in the demo files and there’s a long forgotten piece of music that is 95% album ready. This actually happened on this record. It’s been eight years between Mission Creep and The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams – were you working on the record all this time, or were you focused on other things? Garce: Song writing is a perpetual thing but the other project we’ve worked on over the last three years is the SLAG documentary being produced by Jean Paul Van Mierlo who did the excellent Adrian Borland film Walking in the Opposite Direction. This is with the same film maker Marc Waltman. This is your second record working with Igor Garanin – can you share some stories about working together? Garce: Igor is a mix engineer Tony knows through Above & Beyond and he did such a great job on Mission Creep that we used him again on the new album. Tony works with Igor in the studio and then sends us mixes for comment. How has your songwriting style evolved over the years? Garce: If you mean the way we get to a finished album, then the human process is very similar but the technology available now means we don’t have to do the traditional ‘recording studio’ thing. In that sense, we are effectively self-producing, whereas before, the person paying for the studio, i.e., Nick Ralph if it was Midnight Music, had a large say in the overall production decisions and the ‘style’ of the finished songs. But I think what you mean is the evolution of our style of song. Many other people will have many differing views on this and which album they like best and I accept it has changed subtly from album to album. Not a lot has changed vocally other than I’ve got better at writing melodies and perhaps more focused on saying what I want, in the way I want, in order to compliment the music and bring out the best in a song. Changes in personnel obviously bring an element of change so the key personnel swap was Tony McGuinness for Simon Blanchard on guitar after the second album. I could write an essay on that. Then there was Juliet Sainsbury (currently lives in LA) on keyboards in the eighties, she was the most accomplished keyboardist we’ve had so what she plays the others wouldn’t have been able to. Then we’ve had Cliff Silver on bass replaced by Ian Gibson and both are like chalk and cheese as musicians and songwriters. The net result of all this in my opinion, is that if anything the cinematic quality of the ambient strings and ‘wet’ noise has become more lush and expansive but…to a listener coming to the band now, the songs on the latest album have all the same sonic qualities and idiosyncrasies as all the other albums. We have a distinctive SLAG sound which we understand and respect. Nigel: Our style has not really changed over the years; we all know what makes a good SLAG song . Our songs stand the test of time, and I personally cannot distinguish between songs written 40 years ago to those that are on our latest album. Garce has and continues to write very emotional and evocative lyrics which many fans can connect with. Can you expand on some of the lyrics or themes behind the record? Garce: “We will be ashes, we will be silent and old, we will be wisdom, we will be left in the cold” were the lyrics I wrote as a twenty four year old for our second single “Things We Never Did.” I am now far older than the age I envisaged in that song and I have no intention of being silent or of being left in the cold! Broadly, I would describe my lyrics as ‘English Melancholia’ but I noticed a wry-ness creeping in over the course of this recent album, although given that I am writing about the state of the world as I currently see it there’s precious little to chuckle about; call it gallows humour. As a device, I often write against a fictional dystopian backdrop (“Asylum Town,” “Repentance Day,” “Down To The Wire”), but increasingly the dystopia has become reality since the last album in 2018. Unfortunately, that does seem to be the case, doesn’t it? Sad to think that all the prophecies, whether it be in lyrics or films or literature has come true, in a sense. On a lighter, but related note, what else, other than music, do you tend to draw inspiration from? Garce: Literature and Art Nigel: Differing cultures and the great outdoors. Sad Lovers & Giants have always had such iconic artwork across both your singles and LPs. The covers alone really convey such a strong sense of emotion and perfectly reflect the music in my opinion. I’d love to hear more about what inspires your album artwork. Garce: Simon Blanchard designed the sleeves for the first three singles, including the image for “Lost In a Moment” (girl in armchair with teddy bear!), which is one that is particularly well known. Given that he also wrote much of the songs I think his design choices were intuitively in alignment with his songwriting. Midnight Music did the design work for many subsequent releases but they were building on the foundations he had laid. We asked Simon to design The Weight of Forgotten Dreams as he did such a great job with the previous album, Mission Creep and Cherry Red Records asked him to design the box set they released. Simon: Well it’s imortant to remember I can’t claim credit for all the band’s sleevework and Tony’s contribution is not to be underestimated. It’s not always easy to provide a visual foil for their music, but having been there since the beginning, I probably have a basic understanding of the strange world they inhabit. There’s usually a lot of trial and error and this time it was helpful to have access to some of Garce’s original paintings, which I montaged-up with the photography. To me it felt that the result sat well with the music and luckily the band liked it. Will you be touring for this record? Garce: In SLAG world there are three things happening currently. The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams, the film and then the live double album recorded for the film, so we will be playing live more over the next two years to coincide with this creative phase. I was happy to hear that the band finally came to the US after all these years, but sadly I live in New York and couldn’t make it to the West Coast/Austin shows. Do you plan to come back to North America at all? Garce: We want to come back and at some point over this next two years would be great timing but we are not in any specific discussions at present. Obviously as we did the West Coast plus Canada and SXSW in Austin last time, the East Coast and New York would be a priority next time. In the Breeze-era lineup. Photo by Cliff Ash. Looking back to the formation of the band, can you tell us a bit about how you all came together? Garce: The band was originally formed by Simon, Nigel and Dave Wood, who were at school together. They were called The Traumatics and they recruited an outside bass player called Steve Carter who sadly died quite recently. Dave played tenor sax and both Simon and Steve sang. At that time I was playing guitar (and singing backing vocals) in another local band called Suspect Device and we knew each other from playing together supporting a well known local band called Mr E and The Imaginations. Mr E had supported The Ruts at The Marquee club and the guitarist and singer of The Ruts were at our gig. I knew Dave Wood from drinking and playing pool together at The Feathers in Rickmansworth and he invited me to audition as the singer of The Traumatics. From that first meeting we knew it would work because we shared the same musical tastes. Our first London gigs were performed as The Traumatics with Steve Carter on bass. When we did “50:50” he sang it and I played keyboards. We changed the name from The Traumatics to Sad Lovers & Giants in January 1981. Sometime after the first single we brought in Cliff Silver on bass who we knew from playing with other Watford bands that he was in. We also bought a string synth and Simon began experimenting with spacial guitar sounds. Dave began playing the string synth more than the sax. Simon: We formed pretty soon after the punk explosion in the late seventies. We had been listening to rock music for years before that as young teenagers but it suddenly became very clear that you could be in a band with only very rudimentary music skills. We slowly got better – but not that much. The Traumatics. Photo credit unknown. Mid-80s lineup. Photo by Nick Ralph. Was there a coherent scene in Watford? Garce: There were a lot of young bands who all knew each other and played and drank in the same pubs. There was the Watford Pub Rock competition run by the owner of the local music shop and there were several fanzines. Apart from ‘our sort of music’ i.e. Post Punk/New Wave/Alternative/Art School bands, there were other more mainstream rock and blues bands mainly comprised of older musicians. Watford was a seething mass of music and musicians but probably no different to many large towns in the early eighties. The UK music scene at that time was quite remarkable looking back on it. I listened to a BBC radio 4 programme the other day whose basic premise was that the counterculture of the ’60s didn’t die out but was boosted by punk and morphed into the indie scene of the ’80s. But then the establishment pushed back, Thatcherism (Margaret Thatcher, prime minister 1979 to 1990) was in effect a counter-counterculture where alternative views were discouraged. On the whole we weren’t overtly political but if you were in one of those young bands then you knew who the enemy was and just doing it was resistance of sorts. That was the true source of the apparent coherence. A disparate collection of bands from Watford and nearby towns got together and put out an album called The Thing From The Crypt but the DIY record scene was just a reflex in the instinctive resistance to the establishment. I love that compilation and was very happy to pick up the Dark Entries reissue a few years back! Otherwise, the band has such an iconic catalog of tracks, including bangers like “50:50,” “Seven Kinds of Sin,” “In Flux,” “Colourless Dream,” etc. that are still heard in clubs today. How do you feel about the band’s legacy thus far? Garce: When we started we were defining our sound and every new song we wrote was a step into the unknown. When we reformed in 2009 we were coming off the back of a reputation built over thirty years and eight albums so from then on there was a pressure to maintain the standards we had set. As a live band we’ve surpassed those early standards which comes not only from experience but from having a huge back catalogue of great songs to choose from; we have the songs and we know how to use them. These days we’ve scaled our live show up for some seriously large gigs and have sold out 1200 capacity venues in our own name but we are still a cult band albeit with a huge worldwide following. Sometimes I dream about suddenly becoming a mainstream act but in reality I’m quite happy being where we are. Which begs the question, “if it’s not about world domination what is it about?” Answer: the music, the fans, the international travel, the ‘pinch yourself’ moments when we achieve something surprising like having “Colourless Dream” used in the Netflix Andy Warhol series. But above all it’s about the shared experience of doing it all with your mates and…still being able to make music. As a post punk-eighties band, we are always going to be remembered for those first two albums but there are eight others and Spotify has helped get them heard with around 150,000 plays a month. I’m very proud of all of them; they are all unique and have their own story to tell. The trick with the last two has been to keep our essential ‘sound’ whilst conforming to modern production expectations because fans listen to the work recorded in the analogue world of the early eighties and the production standards of that era were completely different, nevertheless they are synonymous with what the fans think of as SLAG. That is acceptable when it’s tinged with nostalgia but not in the modern world. If I remember correctly there was hardly any compression used on the early albums, can you believe that? So I think The Weight of Forgotten Dreams sits well in the legacy scheme of things. But what next? Do we write one last happy album? Hopefully there will be many more to come! Can you share some personal highlights from over the years? Garce: Showcasing at SXSW in 2016 Nigel: Playing our first gig as Sad Lovers & Giants in our hometown of Rickmansworth, recording our second single (“Colourless Dream”) in Surrey Sound where Siouxsie and the Banshees had been recording their LP Juju. More recently playing to 5,000 people at the 2024 Visor fest in Murcia, Spain, with the Sun going down – Magical! Tony: Highlight for me was selling out Echoplex in LA at the end of our first US tour. Ian: I enjoy playing live so my personal highlights are: The first time we played The Marquee in Wardour Street – I felt it was a proper rock venue that I’d previously been to as a punter, it felt a bit surreal to me to be up on that stage in front of paying punters. Another surreal moment was my overseas debut at Club Isla near Valencia, which felt like an enormous gig to me. The Echoplex in LA was special. The festival in Murcia was too….so many great gigs. SLAG at the Echoplex in 2016. Photo by Terry Howick. Will: Playing live is definitely my favourite part of being in Sad Lovers & Giants. I love meeting the fans and other bands that we play with, I love seeing places around the world from a perspective that I wouldn’t be able to access without the network of promoters and friends that the band cultivates. I love feeling the connection with our audience during a performance – which feels like a celebration of the band, every time, and I feel privileged to be part of it and to help contribute to the legacy. In particular, I will always remember our US tour – which was a huge undertaking for the band – a chaotic yet rewarding experience of massive drives, downtown motels and passionate crowds. What’s next for the band? Garce: We play two gigs in Italy this October, then we put the final touches to the film for the rest of this year. The live album will be pressed and ready for release around then but the exact timing of everything depends on the film. Then we have a gig on a boat in Paris in March followed hopefully by a small tour of Portugal and Spain. After that there will inevitably be a series of gigs in all the usual places, namely Holland, Germany and Greece. Meanwhile the demo file will begin filling up again! § Sad Lovers & Giants’ new album The Weight of Forgotten Dreams is out now! Listen via Spotify and order here. Follow Sad Lovers & Giants Linktree Website Instagram Facebook Spotify Documentary Kickstarter Header photo by Simon Blanchard The post Down To The Wire — An Interview With Sad Lovers & Giants appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items._cn_summary: 该乐评以回顾Sad Lovers & Giants的职业生涯为主线，叙述乐队自1980年成立以来在英伦后朋克场景中的演变，包括早期作品、原始阵容变动、1987年重组后对梦幻流行运动的启发，以及2002年再度复出后的持续活动。文章强调乐队保持了一贯的氛围化声响与爆炸性现场表现，并提及最新专辑《The Weight of Forgotten Dreams》收录十首新作，延续其宏大音色与情绪张力。但乐评并未深入剖析具体曲目或声响细节，更多是作为乐队历史综述和new release公告，缺乏对音乐本体之实验性或融合性的具体讨论。

items.body: Four years ago Intibint started making a record she wasn’t sure anyone would fund. Last July she threw a fundraiser for it on her own birthday, at The Rum Shack in Glasgow’s Southside with the Arab club night WSHWSH, and told the room that the politics in her work might cost her the grant she was applying for. She got there in the end, politics and all: Half Moon Eyes comes out on 18 September through Bandcamp and SoundCloud and nowhere else, played live first at Ormside Projects in London tomorrow and Stereo in Glasgow on Saturday. Born in London, raised between there and Sanaa and now in Glasgow, she wrote the album across Yemen, Egypt, Slovakia, England and Scotland and produced, recorded and mixed every part of it herself. Travelling, she records what she hears: that’s how trains, fireworks and dolphins from those journeys run through “Dolphin”, gunshots from Yemeni celebration footage inside “Disrespectful af”, a Glasgow trans rights protest from 2025 opening “S.A.B.R”. “Disrespectful af” was built out of an argument in which she was called disrespectful for naming racism, and “Hayati”, the one song out before release, came from working out in Glasgow that a Yemeni woman could live a life for herself. She sings in Arabic and English across the album, close to the microphone, repeating her lines, over nocturnal pop chords and production that moves between downtempo, alt-R&B, grime and EBM, with Arabic modal writing under most of it. Live, she performs from CDJs most nights, though for these two launches three musicians join her on stage. Ekin Oykener, the Cypriot musician who plays oud on the album’s “Sunflower” and “S.A.B.R”, takes guitar and oud, and Fatma Hegazy, an Egyptian-Scottish artist trained on classical guitar who also DJs at both nights, takes the other guitar, completing the line-up with Nadine on drums. Between her own songs she reaches for revolutionary ones from Yemen, Palestine and Sudan. Tomorrow’s London show is put on by grassroots promoter flowers.ldn with WSHWSH, at Ormside Projects. The arts centre has run out of a unit in the Penarth Centre off Old Kent Road since 2015, Arts Council funded, showing films, mounting exhibitions and listening parties, running workshops and a photography studio, and handing the room over most weekends to independent promoters working the experimental end of electronic music: industrial and deconstructed club, dub techno, gqom and hard drum, footwork and jungle. flowers.ldn and WSHWSH are behind Saturday’s show too, at Stereo in Glasgow, which took over the ground floor and basement of Mackintosh’s Daily Record building on Renfield Lane in 2007. A vegan cafe bar runs upstairs and the gigs happen in the space below, programmed heavily towards queer and marginalised artists and the experimental end of club music: dubstep and grime, jungle and drum and bass, baile funk, ballroom, MENA and SWANA club nights. Four DJs play both nights, either side of the live set. Salam Kitty co-founded WSHWSH after starting the Scottish QTIPoC+ party Mojxmma, and plays bass-heavy percussive club music with Afro-electro and leftfield techno in it. Nihal El Aasar grew up in Cairo, writes from London, and spends her monthly NTS show Nile to Bank following left-field hip hop, drill and drum and bass out of the Middle East and North Africa. MAVEEN and Fatma Hegazy fill out both bills, Fatma opening tonight before she picks up the guitar later, with candice a.m in London and unknown niece, who co-created flowers.ldn, in Glasgow. Half Moon Eyes is out on the 18th, but you can hear it live first: Ormside tomorrow, doors at 7pm with Intibint on at 21:20, then Stereo on Saturday from half nine. Nobody gets turned away for lack of funds, so if you are on Universal Credit, seeking asylum or just short, message the promoters and you are on the door.   Tickets are on sale for tomorrow in London and Saturday in Glasgow   The post Event Preview: Intibint @ Ormside Projects (London; Thursday 10th September 2026) & Stereo (Glasgow; Saturday 12th September 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Being a robust rebel is fully explained by my Prog Rogue moniker and there is no intention ever to alter that mindset. Receiving music from any hitherto unknown musician often reveals somewhere along the line a few connections, whether in style, in associations or guest artists. It was therefore easy to agree to getting the download done when the name Rob Harrison from Z Machine showed up in the EPK. Lester drums for that band. Bingo! The dots are connected. Even though my personal prog shrine remains deeply entrenched in melodic and symphonic stylistics, there is no way that I would contemplate not tasting material outside of the comfort zone I am most familiar with. In fact, recently dabbling in dungeon synth artists, darkwave, and folk-metal as well as continuously listening to jazz, experimental and electronic provide a very wide berth of interest. This release typically required an initial listen to reformulate the ears into an altogether different mindset and a third revisit confirmed my thoughts as well as dispelling any misgivings. The Rogue enjoys being challenged, musically and otherwise. Sometimes thought-provoking music can come across as masturbatory displays of ego-driven chopzilla (as I witnessed sadly at a 1973 Return to Forever concert, opening for Focus of all people, and Stanley Clarke's spot was so crass that the devout fans started booing him). This is absolutely not the case anywhere on this album. Let us dive in, so to speak. "Anaraknophobia" could very well be a fear of spiders that thrive in a polar anorak , only Lester knows for sure. This is a great introductory piece that combines sturdy bass playing, brass instruments and electric guitars , as well as the percussive talents of the man in question, providing some vibraphone inserts as well . Its very modern jazz, with overt influences of that glorious Brit jazz-rock school I particularly cherish with well-heeled names like Soft Machine, Hatfield and the North, Nucleus, Neil Ardley, Gilgamesh, Penguin Caf� Orchestra, In Cahoots, Catapilla, Blue Drift, Turning Point, Back Door and many others. So let that sink in before plunging headfirst into the colossal maelstrom that is the title track, a nearly 22-minute behemoth of bedazzling authority, stunning contrasts, roller coaster rides well within the free jazz lineage. It's a master class of impeccable musicianship on a collective basis being the core strength attribute of jazz but where the solo spots are deeply entangled within the endless succession of variations, shifts, moods and atmospheres, every player taking a turn with the ball. Needless to state that this performance is worthy of the loftiest praise, placing this arrangement, an undeniably accurate comment may I add , on the same altar ruled by the previously mentioned stalwarts. The immediate impression is one of a sonic mosaic composed of a myriad of little details that interlock perfectly like an Inca jigsaw puzzle, a cinematographic soundtrack that may leave one confounded but never confused. Close your eyes, open your ears and imagine a place where speed, silk, swing, serenity, stupefaction race along the canals of your mind, finished off by a niggling hint of argy-bargy (i.e my favourite British word), rekindling a kind recollection of a Rob Harrison album title called "Explode My Head" ! Where the hell is my jaw, I can't seem to find it anymore ! And to blur the issue even further, "Moonfire" is a giant leap sideways into more ambient realms, influenced by that classic SM track off Softs "Song of Aeolus", a pastoral promenade that glitters gently like a sunny day in Albion, a gorgeous melodic asteroid of celestial joy, unpretentiously pretty and heartfelt. Really worth holding onto. Thanks to an unexpected typo (are they not always unforeseen?), "Worth Holding Onto" has a garrulously rumbling bass leading the way, galloping all over the green valleys and glimmering meadows, with more stop and starts than a failing computer. Utterly playful, especially for a bass fanatic like me, I literally got off on this track, what a ride. The melodicism surfaces once again on "Joining the Q", a line that dares to go around the entire block, keeping the easy-going patients entertained as they await their turn. The super cool vibraphone spot comes in to wink at the crowd, the bass burping delectably, and Lester doing his Buddy Rich thingy, shuffles and ruffles galore. Just when one feels comfortable in getting the true meaning of an album, Lester takes this once again into a "Mountain Pass", a short sonic slash between peaks that has the audacity to combine Celtic bliss with rapid-fire percussive agility! That's right folks, it's his mini-solo spotlight! Fabulous. Finishing in style with a funky dispatch and perhaps waving mean polkadot handkerchiefs "Mister Meaner" has all the urban charm of a vivacious late afternoon romp around the various sites and sound of happy place, everyone smiling and content with the niceties of life (like great music). That insistent bass has totally seduced me, I must admit, I think I have fallen in love. The breezy keys, the daring electric guitar solo and the brass work are all the added spice one can ask for. And now, for the coup de grace (Pronounced "koo de grass" for you anglophiles ): all the instrumentation, recording , arranging and producing was undertaken by one Lester Greenhalgh . Golden buzzer. 4.5 hard machines

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由鼓手Lester Greenhalgh领衔的现代爵士融合专辑。乐评人因吉他手Rob Harrison来自Z Machine乐队这一关联而接触此作，开篇曲《Anaraknophobia》便展示了贝斯、铜管、电吉他与颤音琴的立体编织，承袭了英国爵士摇滚学派的深厚传统，与Soft Machine、Nucleus、Gilgamesh等经典团体的审美血脉相连。同名标题曲以近22分钟的篇幅展开自由爵士式的壮阔图景，多位乐手轮流主导独奏段落，音乐在持续变化中维持张力与流畅的平衡。整体呈现为一部精密协作的集体即兴作品，细节如印加拼图般精确咬合，体现了深厚的演奏功底与成熟的作曲架构。
