items.body: Review by andrea — "Mass-Media Stars" is the second album by Acqua Fragile and was released in 1974 on the Ricordi label with a confirmed line up featuring Bernardo Lanzetti (vocals, guitar), Gino Campanini (electric and acoustic guitar, vocals), Maurizio Mori (keyboards, vocals), Franz Dondi (bass) and Pier Emilio Canavera (drums, acoustic guitar, vocals). The album, produced by Claudio Fabi (best known for his work with PFM), has a good sound quality and the musicians seem more aware of their songwriting abilities. In my opinion, the tracks on it sound more personal and mature if compared with those on their self-titled debut. However, the final outcome is somewhat hampered by the band's stubbornness in insisting on singing their songs in English, against the wishes of their record company and an Italian market that was at the time unreceptive to such a proposal. This led to a commercial flop, despite the quality of the album...The fine opening track, "Cosmic Mind Affair", evokes astronomical laws that serve as a guide for our minds, inviting us on a journey into the depths of the cosmos while walking on the thin line of madness. The mysteries of the universe are too profound to be fathomed or understood by our limited human capabilities: what if we were nothing more than strange, incredible creatures generated by the brains of other worlds? Like the aliens that populate our dreams...The following "Bar Gazing" is at times musically reminiscent of Genesis while its somewhat surreal lyrics draw inspiration from the observation of the customers of a bar located in a town square. An unruly driver, a bee inspector, a couple of pharmacy lovers...The instrumental intro to "Mass-Media Stars" is strongly reminiscent of PFM. Then, the festive atmosphere is paired with sarcastic lyrics about rock stars and their diva-like attitudes: vain artists who bark loudly in the air, with a political touch and the gift of the gab; frivolous Lolitas who think they can do rock'n'roll better than Elvis while flaunting a thousand gimmicks that you have to admire with the blessing of the media..."Opening Act" starts by a vocal part a cappella that might bring Gentle Giant to mind, but the music soon shifts toward a West Coast sound. The track brilliantly and wryly depicts life on the road for an obscure rock band trying to make a name for itself by opening the concerts for major stars. There are no press clippings about the unknown band, no groupies waiting for them, no personal roadies and their cheap instruments keep going out of tune. Yet, every night brings the thrill of performing, fuelled by the hope of catching the audience's eye and perhaps even getting called back for an encore..."Professor" is an interesting, caustic piece that paints in music and words the portrait of an austere, know-it-all man who delights in picking out others' mistakes and point out what an artist is lacking; a ruthless critic who poses as an expert without truly being one. With weary eyes and a black bow tie, he takes pleasure in denigrating the work of others. Yet, one has to wonder: what is the point of dwelling on trivial errors when it would be far more useful to highlight what is actually working? The protagonist is merely a professor who teaches nothing; his petty attitude will ultimately lead him into oblivion, while the people he criticised go on with all their mistakes and their enthusiasm...The last track, "Coffee Song", is a melancholic acoustic ballad about the passing of time and the need to be ready for every new opportunity - despite any despondency or sadness - because there is nothing worse than looking back with regret at having lost the winning path simply because one was tired...On the whole, a very good work.
items._genre: Rock Progressivo Italiano / progressive rock / symphonic rock
items._cn_summary: 意大利前卫摇滚乐队Acqua Fragile的第二张专辑，延续七十年代RPI风格，音乐在Genesis、PFM与Gentle Giant之间游走，旋律与编曲较首专更成熟。全英文演唱导致与本土市场脱节，未能获得商业成功。开篇曲以宇宙法则隐喻心智边界；随后描绘酒吧众生相、讽刺媒体包装下的明星做派、无名乐队巡演的辛酸，以及装腔作势的批评家形象。制作人Claudio Fabi曾与PFM合作，录音质感良好。乐队坚持使用英语被视为市场受阻主因，但专辑本身具备一定的艺术完成度。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — This short-lived mysterious act that emerged from Pushkin, a nearby suburb of St Petersburg, Russiais the epitome of obscurity having only released its sole effort Литургия безумия / A LITURGY OFMADNESS in 1991 and then never to be heard from again. Given it debuted during the tumultuous timewhen the Soviet Union was collapsing into the Russian Federation and outlying nations, the band andalbum has become a very forgotten entry in the region's rich musical history. This psychedelicprogressive band was the trio of bassist Aleksandr Berezkin, guitarist Aleksey Romanov and drummerIvan Fedenko, the latter of which was a seasoned Soviet musician having played in the new wave actAVIA as well as the jazz fusion ensemble Junglie.Together this triumvirate of instrumental experimental prog crafted an album's worth of complexpsychedelia where classic prog nods effortlessly free flow through an album's worth of psychedelichaze augmented by Beefheart inspired angularities and Pink Floyd infused grooviness. Whiletechnically hosting 13 individual tracks, the album can rightfully be thought of as two side-longtracks that offer variations on a theme to transition from one motif and cadence to the nextoffering moments of high energy rock along with an ever-changing rotisserie of time signatures,tempos, tones and progressive weavings. The album has been cited as catering the melodic prowess ofclassic Yes recordings laced with off-kilter avant-progeny angularities that sprang into existenceat the end of the 1970s but this is very subtle in actuality.Beginning with the raucous ride that constitutes side one, the wily suite "Бешеный Огурец, Часть 1 /Mad Cucumber, Part" displays a fertile musical fecundity in action where essentially a jam bandchannels its inner prog credentials and takes a five-part journey through musical terrains thatemulate past masters but yet sound like none of them. A crafty and creative wild ride through mostlyguitar-driven / keyboard-free excursions through meandering musical motifs, A LITURGY OF MADNESSdespite it's title and insinuations that it will be a dark journey of the soul actually comes off asmore light-hearted and stews in the broth of psychedelia more than the underbelly of the earlyUnivers Zero playbook yet many nods to avant-prog masters of yore insert their angular angles intothe overall context. Some clear King Crimson references also are in the overall fabric.Although some will claim the album is a continuous flow from beginning to end, in reality the firstside is clearly delineated from the second with "Бешеный Огурец, Часть 2 / Mad Cucumber, Part 2"taking on a distinctly different mood setting although in general the same meandering unpredictableprocession of what sounds like aimless musically lollygagging that somehow flows organically andwithout startling unrelated transitions. Despite the avant-prog reference the music is overall moreon the melodic side but creatively distinct as not really pointing to many other bands that hademerged up to this point in the prog timeline. For the most part this is a subtle release thatdoesn't offer a lot in terms of timbres and instrumental offerings with all the creative effortstucked into the varying motifs that span on for a 40 1/2 minute mind journey. This is one that tooka few spins to sink in but ultimately delivers a nice meandering package of highly idiosyncraticpsychedelia that sounds fairly unique.
items._genre: psychedelic rock / progressive rock / avant-prog / space rock
items._cn_summary: 这张1991年苏联解体时期由圣彼得堡郊区三人组合创作的唯一专辑，是冷战后俄罗斯地下音乐史中极为冷门的一笔。贝斯手、吉他手与鼓手共同构建了长达两张唱片长度的迷幻前卫之旅，以吉他为主导、刻意回避键盘的编配贯穿始终。作品中可见对Yes旋律功底、King Crimson棱角分明的和声、Captain Beefheart式不规则节拍以及Pink Floyd律动感的多元致敬。整张专辑虽分13首曲目，实则可分为两个长篇组曲，各自展开不同主题与情绪弧线。前半段偏向高能量的jammish即兴穿梭，融入大量不规则拍号与节奏变速；后半段则转向更为内省的氛围营造。虽然标题暗示这是一段黑暗的灵魂之旅，实际音乐却偏向轻盈与迷幻色彩，avant-prog的影响虽存在但处理得相当克制。对于偏爱前卫摇滚及其衍生实验方向的听众，这是一份值得考古式发掘的历史遗珠。

items.body: Uredda, a new Italian-based project built around members of Zu and Coil/Spiritualized veteran Thighpaulsandra, has released “All He Knows” as the first single from its debut album, “Nüwa Mends the Sky”. The album is due December 4 via House of Mythology on black and clear vinyl LP, CD digipak and digital formats. The single arrives with an official music video. Uredda brings together Thighpaulsandra (vocals, synthesizers, piano, organ, mellotron), Mariagiulia Degli Amori (vocals, percussion, electronics), Bruno Germano (guitars, vocals), Paolo Mongardi (drums, percussion, vocals) and Massimo Pupillo (bass, vocals). Pupillo and Mongardi are also members of the Roman instrumental trio Zu, while Thighpaulsandra previously played in Coil and Spiritualized. The band’s sound mixes electronics, new wave, post-punk, krautrock and drone. ‘Nüwa Mends the Sky’ due December 4 via House of Mythology “Nüwa Mends the Sky” holds five tracks: “All He Knows,” “Dress To The Right,” “Blonde Charger,” “Tāne Obelisk” and “From the Ivy Bowl.” Uredda’s own Bandcamp listing and label coverage of the announcement both describe this as the album’s complete tracklist. The official video for “All He Knows” was uploaded to House of Mythology’s YouTube channel. It can be watched below. Nüwa Mends the Sky by Uredda Speaking about the release of “All He Knows,” Pupillo stated: “All I know is that a world on the precipice has a desperate need for beauty. Not a shallow and only cosmetic glamour, but real beauty – one that incorporates and transforms our deepest anxieties and fears. The diamond is born in the lotus, but the lotus is born from the mud.” “Nüwa Mends the Sky” can be pre-ordered through the House of Mythology store. About Uredda Uredda formed in Italy in 2026 out of an unplanned studio session. Thighpaulsandra had traveled to the country for a solo performance when Massimo Pupillo and Paolo Mongardi, working on new material at guitarist Bruno Germano’s studio, invited him to join them. Mariagiulia Degli Amori completed the lineup, and the resulting sessions became “Nüwa Mends the Sky” without prior rehearsal or a fixed plan for a band. Thighpaulsandra, born Timothy Lewis, began working with Julian Cope’s touring band in the late 1980s before joining Spiritualized in 1997, where he stayed until 2008 and appeared on releases including “Let It Come Down” and “Amazing Grace.” In 1998 he joined Coil, performing on “Astral Disaster” and both volumes of “Musick to Play in the Dark” alongside Peter Christopherson and John Balance. He also records with Pupillo in the duo URUK, which has released two albums since 2017. Pupillo and Mongardi play together in Zu, the Rome-founded instrumental trio formed in 1997 that also includes Luca Mai on baritone saxophone; Mongardi joined Zu’s lineup in 2011. The name Uredda comes from the “Caso Amicizia” (“Friendship Case”), an Italian account of alleged contact between humans and beings known as W56 in Abruzzo between 1956 and the late 1970s, in which “Uredda” denoted the vital energy of love and friendship. With “All He Knows” out now and “Nüwa Mends the Sky” set for December 4, Uredda’s debut marks the first joint release from this Zu-Thighpaulsandra lineup.

items.body: Swedish composer David Granström has released the single “A Shadow Cast”, the opening track from his new album “Echoes of Impermanence,” due November 6 on XKatedral as a CD and digital release. “Echoes of Impermanence” is Granström’s fourth full-length, following “Ephemeris” (2016) and “A Distant Color, Secluded” (2019) on XKatedral, and “Empty Room” on Hallow Ground. The album marks a shift in his sound: the electric guitar enters his previously hermetic, minimalist compositions built from long-duration digital synthesis, pushing a riff-driven character to the surface that had stayed submerged in his earlier work. Granström recorded the album at Elektronmusikstudion EMS and in his own studio, with help from Mats Erlandsson, who also mastered the record. Long-time collaborator and XKatedral co-founder Maria W Horn guests on Hurdy-Gurdy on the title track, “Echoes of Impermanence.” Granström plays guitar, synthesizers, zither and drums throughout. All guitars were recorded by Erlandsson at EMS except on “Ossarium,” and the closing track, “A Light Radiates Into Tomorrow,” was originally commissioned by Fylkingen. Photography for the release is by Aron Mattsson, with sleeve design by Stephen O’Malley. The tracklist for “Echoes of Impermanence” runs: A Shadow Cast Echoes of Impermanence Ossarium To Fade Away Draped Urn A Light Radiates Into Tomorrow A Shadow Cast by David Granström About David Granström David Granström is a composer and musician from Umeå, in the north of Sweden, a city with a stronghold of extreme musical expression. He grew up playing guitar in a metal band and began composing within that context, work that evolved into solo projects once he gained access to studio facilities next to his rehearsal space. Granström found his own musical voice in electroacoustic composition, applying his programming background to build sound and form governed by algorithmic processes, resulting in music defined by harmonic simplicity paired with spatiotextural complexity, mixing synthetic and acoustic sources with strict digital synthesis techniques. He released his debut album, “Ephemeris,” on XKatedral in October 2016, followed by “A Distant Color, Secluded” on the same label in November 2019, an edition of 300 built from four interrelated pieces. “Empty Room,” recorded between 2019 and 2020, followed on the Hallow Ground label in 2021. Granström also appears on “XKatedral Anthology Series III,” the label’s double-vinyl tenth-anniversary compilation released in May 2026 alongside label figures including Kali Malone, Maria W Horn, Jessica Ekomane and Stephen O’Malley. “Echoes of Impermanence,” out November 6, continues that run and adds the electric guitar to his compositional language for the first time.
items._genre: electroacoustic / experimental / contemporary classical / drone / dark ambient
items._cn_summary: 瑞典作曲家David Granström即将发行第四张全长专辑《Echoes of Impermanence》，收录六首作品。该专辑延续了此前的电子音乐创作脉络，将长时间数字合成构建的极简主义作曲法与新加入的电吉他相结合，形成riff驱动的听觉质感。录制工作分别在其个人工作室与斯德哥尔摩电子音乐工作室EMS完成，吉他部分由长期合作者Mats Erlandsson在该场地录制。专辑同名曲邀请XKatedral联合创始人Maria W Horn演奏Hurdy-Gurdy，封面摄影与设计分别由Aron Mattsson与Stephen O'Malley完成。其音乐风格以电子声响与原声乐器的交织为基础，强调和声简洁性与时空质感复杂度。

items.album: SIERRA VEINS interview: ‘Safe enough to let go of some of that control’

items.body: There is a productive contradiction at the centre of SIERRA VEINS: what can appear almost uncontrolled onstage depends on an unusually rigorous degree of preparation. Lighting cues and instrumental parts are fixed in advance, yet the security of that technical structure is precisely what allows the performance to become less predictable, more physical and more responsive to the room. The same relationship between control and surrender exists in the writing process. Images, colours, places and even titles can precede the music itself, so the visual world is not something designed afterwards to illustrate finished songs; it belongs to the same compositional vocabulary from the beginning. That interconnected thinking became particularly explicit on “In The Name Of Blood”, SIERRA VEINS’ second album, released in November 2025. Its exploration of identity, inheritance and DNA coincided with the transition from SIERRA to SIERRA VEINS, while the recurring image of veins and cables allows biology and technology to occupy the same visual language. The album also reflects how profoundly performing has altered the way SIERRA composes: although the stage is not allowed to dictate the writing, certain moments were deliberately created with physical performance in mind. That tension between human instability and machine precision extends well beyond the album. In February 2026, SIERRA VEINS released the 19-track “HypnoVizion 031: SIERRA VEINS” DJ mix, using selection and sequencing to expose musical interests that extend outside her own production, while January 2027 will bring her first Australian dates alongside Carpenter Brut, revisiting an artistic relationship that previously produced “Power”. I spoke with SIERRA VEINS just a while before her performance at Nocuturnal Culture Night Festival in Deutzen – about why artistic abandon requires technical security, composing simultaneously through sound and images, allowing the body to influence electronic music, the changing meaning of songs once they reach the stage, collaboration as a question of shared emotional language, and why the next significant evolution of SIERRA VEINS may happen visually before it happens musically. In The Name Of Blood by SIERRA VEINS Sierra Veins interview Karo: I have seen you live several times now, and one thing that keeps fascinating me is that I never feel I am watching exactly the same show twice. The visual language is recognisable, the songs are familiar, but the physical intensity, the movement and even the way the light seems to interact with you change every time. How much of a SIERRA VEINS performance is actually fixed, and how much is allowed to mutate according to the room, the audience and your own state that night? Is there a carefully constructed structure that gives you the freedom to become almost wild inside it? SIERRA VEINS: I’m glad to hear that. My live show is very structured: the lighting and the parts I play with my instruments are predetermined in advance, but there are many things that can vary from one show to another, beyond simply the selection of songs, and make the experience different. The size of the venue, the location or type of festival, the lighting and sound setup, which can change from one place to another, and of course my own performance all have an influence. From one night to another, depending on how I feel and what is happening in the moment, I can interpret a song in one way or another. Karo: You have said that when you begin an album, you often start with atmosphere, images and mood boards before the actual composition, and that with “In The Name Of Blood” the visual world of blood, veins, cables and green existed very early in the process. That makes me wonder whether “visuals” is even the right word, because it suggests something added to music afterwards. Do you experience light, colour, sound and movement as separate elements at all, or are you effectively composing one work in several sensory languages? SIERRA VEINS: Indeed, all the EPs and albums I’ve released so far were written with a universe already in my mind. I often have images, colours, places or even song and album titles in mind before I actually start writing them. Bringing all these ideas together allows me to create a kind of starting point that then guides the way I compose and gives a direction to the whole project. So I don’t really separate the music from everything that surrounds it. For me, it’s all part of the same universe and everything develops together. Karo: There is a contradiction in your stage presence that I find particularly interesting. From the audience it can look uncontrolled, extremely physical, almost feral, yet you have said that when the organisation is precise, the equipment works and everything around the performance is properly under control, your performance becomes much stronger. Does abandon actually require discipline? Do you need to construct a completely safe technical framework before you can allow yourself to become unsafe artistically? SIERRA VEINS: That’s exactly it. When I feel confident and reassured by the technical side of things, and when I feel that the situation is under control, that’s when I can completely let go and feel much freer on stage. I think it’s the same with my writing process. The moments when I manage to go where I really want to go creatively are the moments when I feel safe enough to let go of some of that control. Karo: You have also explained that you thought much more about live performance while writing “In The Name Of Blood”, particularly creating room to move away from the machines and towards the audience. That is interesting because it reverses the usual process of making a record and then figuring out how to perform it. Has the body now entered your compositional thinking from the beginning? When you write something new, do you already know what you will physically need to do with it onstage? SIERRA VEINS: When I started SIERRA VEINS, I didn’t actually intend to perform live. I wrote my first EPs without thinking about any of this, and I was very far from those considerations. Then, little by little, as I started playing more shows, I realised that some tracks that work well on record don’t necessarily translate as well on stage. And the opposite is also true: some tracks that have a strong impact live aren’t necessarily the most listened to. Today, I don’t want those considerations to be at the centre of my mind when I’m writing, but I do like to keep a few ideas about the live show in the back of my mind while I compose. On my latest album, there are definitely some moments that I wrote specifically with the stage in mind. But it’s still very difficult to know in advance how a track will translate live. You only really discover that once you start performing it and seeing how it feels on stage and how the audience responds to it. Karo: The current stage design uses cables as part of the language of veins, blood and identity, but I also read those cables in another way: they belong equally to electronic machinery. The image is simultaneously biological and technological. Is that ambiguity interesting to you? Your music is created electronically, but your performance is intensely bodily; do you see SIERRA VEINS as existing somewhere in that tension between machine precision and the instability of a human body? SIERRA VEINS: Yes, that ambiguity is definitely something that interests me. I’m fascinated by digital art, technology, computer-based music and all of that, but at the same time, it’s very important to me that human emotions remain at the centre of what I write. It’s quite similar on stage. I wouldn’t want to spend an entire 1h10 show behind my machines. I like the idea that my live shows alternate between moments that are purely electronic, where I’m interacting with my machines, and other moments that are more stripped back technologically, with more space for my voice and my physical presence on stage. That contrast between the human and the machine is important to me. Karo: You once said that it is difficult to generalise about audiences from one country to another because the energy can change completely from one concert to the next. Having watched you more than once, that makes sense to me because your performance seems unusually responsive to the immediate space. What actually changes you most: the size of the stage, proximity of the audience, the architecture of the venue, technical limitations, or simply the energy coming back at you? Have you ever walked onstage with one idea of what the concert would be and realised within the first few minutes that the room required something completely different? SIERRA VEINS: I would say the technical aspect is probably what can influence my performance the most. My show is quite demanding technically, both in terms of lighting and sound. And as I mentioned earlier, if I don’t feel confident for one reason or another, my performance on stage will definitely be affected. My energy and mental space might be entirely focused on making sure that everything runs properly from a technical point of view. Then I would say that what can vary the most is the energy coming from the audience. And that really depends on the configuration and size of the venue, the time of the show, etc. There are no rules. But one thing is certain: the more responsive the audience is, the more energy I give on stage. And yes, it happens very often that I walk on stage and, after a few songs, realise that it’s not at all what I expected. You can never really know in advance. Karo: “In The Name Of Blood” deals with identity, inheritance, DNA and the uncomfortable question of how much of ourselves is chosen and how much is already carried within us; even the transition from SIERRA to SIERRA VEINS became part of that idea. But then you have spent months performing those questions repeatedly in front of strangers. Has the live cycle changed your own relationship with the album’s subject? I wonder whether performing a work about identity night after night makes that identity feel more settled, or whether repetition reveals that it is actually much less stable than you thought. SIERRA VEINS: Performing the album on stage for the past few months hasn’t really changed the way I see the questions around identity that I explore on the album. However, my relationship with the songs can change a lot through performing them. Some of them take on a different dimension on stage, and some that I may have felt less attached to at first become very important in the live show, and vice versa. So I would say that it’s not necessarily my perception of my own identity that evolves through performing, but rather my relationship with certain songs. Karo: Your most recent release is “HypnoVizion 031: SIERRA VEINS”, a 19-track DJ mix for HypnoVizion. I find that format interesting in relation to your own records because an album constructs identity through sounds you create, whereas a DJ mix can construct identity through choices, transitions and relationships between other people’s music. What can you say about yourself through selection that you perhaps cannot say through composition? Do you consider sequencing and juxtaposition another form of authorship? SIERRA VEINS: I think DJ mixes are mostly a way for me to show a broader range of my musical tastes. I listen to a lot of music that is quite different from what I produce myself, so it’s a good opportunity to share that side of what I like. There is obviously a creative process in selecting tracks, finding the right transitions and building a progression throughout a mix, so yes, I think it can be a form of authorship, but it’s really difficult to compare it to composing music. Karo: Collaboration has appeared repeatedly in your work, from HEALTH, Carpenter Brut and Gunship around “A Story Of Anger” to Ghost Dance on “Memory Cells” from “In The Name Of Blood”. What makes a collaboration genuinely worthwhile to you? Is the most interesting collaborator someone who understands your language immediately, or someone who introduces an element that initially feels incompatible with it? In other words, are you looking for recognition or productive friction? SIERRA VEINS: A collaboration is really worthwhile when you feel there is an artistic understanding. For me, the most interesting collaborator is someone who speaks the same artistic language, and I don’t necessarily mean having the same artistic universe. I mean someone who understands the emotion, the vibe, even if our universes can sometimes be very different. For me, a good collaboration is mostly about communication and understanding each other from the start. Karo: You have now announced your first Australian tour for 2027 supporting Carpenter Brut, which gives another chapter to a creative relationship that already includes “Power”. Does returning to the same artistic relationship years later feel different once both artists have moved forward? And does touring together create possibilities that a studio collaboration does not, perhaps even for something new to emerge between the projects? SIERRA VEINS: A lot has changed since we first worked on “Power”. The last time we toured together, I hadn’t released an album yet and I had much less experience on stage. So going to Australia together several years later will obviously be a very different experience, and I’m really looking forward to it. As for new collaborations, I’d be very happy to work together again. We’ll see what happens! Karo: You said earlier this year that you were still composing, experimenting with new sounds and working on remixes, but that you deliberately did not want to rush into defining the next release; interestingly, you have also said that although you do not yet know what form that next release will take, you already know something about its visual direction, its colours and its vocabulary. So perhaps this is the right place to finish: when you imagine the next version of SIERRA VEINS, what feels as though it actually needs to change? Is the next step primarily musical, visual, performative, collaborative, or are you beginning to imagine a form in which those distinctions no longer make much sense? SIERRA VEINS: I’m taking a lot of time to experiment with different things, think, and figure out where I want to go next. It’s still a little unclear, but I’m moving forward with my research. Maybe my answer will be different in a few months, but right now, I think the next evolution of the project will probably be more on the visual and graphic side. I won’t say more for now. About SIERRA VEINS SIERRA VEINS is a Paris-based French electronic artist whose work moves through darkwave, EBM, synthwave, techno and heavier electronic forms. The project began in 2017 under the name SIERRA, after a period devoted to learning electronic production, and developed through releases including “Strange Valley,” “Gone” and the 2023 full-length “A Story Of Anger.” The change from SIERRA to SIERRA VEINS was announced in 2025; rather than signalling a musical reinvention, the new name gave a more individual identity to the project and coincided naturally with the themes of inheritance, blood and identity explored on the second album. Released on 7 November 2025, “In The Name Of Blood” centres on identity and the inherited information carried through DNA, with the name change itself incorporated into the album’s creative framework. The record includes “Memory Cells,” created with Ghost Dance, while earlier work has connected SIERRA VEINS with artists including Carpenter Brut, HEALTH and Gunship. Her catalogue has increasingly developed in parallel with an elaborate performance language in which lighting, electronic machinery, voice and movement are conceived as interconnected rather than supplementary elements. That approach is particularly visible in the current “In The Name Of Blood” show, where the visual vocabulary of veins and cables deliberately collapses the distinction between the biological and technological body. In February 2026 she released the 19-track, 46-minute “HypnoVizion 031: SIERRA VEINS” DJ mix, combining her own music with selections from artists including Boys Noize, Matteo Tura, Corvad, Ghost Dance and others. In January 2027, SIERRA VEINS will travel to Australia with Carpenter Brut, joining the project for shows in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne before both appear at Froth & Fury Festival in Adelaide. The dates extend a collaboration that previously resulted in “Power” and arrive at a point when SIERRA VEINS is deliberately resisting the pressure to define her next release too quickly. For the moment, she suggests that the next substantial transformation may take place first in the project’s visual and graphic language rather than through an immediately identifiable musical shift.

items.body: Went out three nights in a row Didn’t know what was About to unfold Subject Sue began as an alter ego, but the separation between performer and person has apparently thinned, and you can hear that collapse in the way these songs handle intimacy. Desire becomes partly theatrical, partly confessional, and sometimes faintly ridiculous, which is exactly right. Clubs have always encouraged people to invent themselves for a few hours, then sent them home with makeup fading in the taxi mirror and a head full of decisions that seemed better under red light. Nightlife, in turn, is a place where fantasy and loneliness can occupy the same square meter. Subject Sue’s Details In The Dark feels built for the hour when the club has stopped pretending to be a social space and has become something more private, a room full of people moving beside one another while each carries a separate crisis under the skin. The Amsterdam artist works in that unstable zone between desire and estrangement, where a glance across the floor can feel intimate for thirty seconds and absurdly remote by the time the bass turns over again. Across six tracks, Sue treats darkwave and ethereal techno less as genres than as materials she can bend around a voice that never sounds entirely convinced by the scene surrounding it. The synthesizers are dense without turning blunt, the percussion keeps its discipline, and the vocals drift above the machinery with a cool distance that makes every romantic gesture feel temporary. There is pleasure everywhere, though it comes with the suspicion that pleasure has already started charging interest. In Details In The Dark, synth lines stretch wide, then recede; voices stack until they resemble memories arguing over the same event; beats keep moving with the indifferent authority of a machine that has seen a thousand romances begin and collapse before breakfast. Sue’s music carries the cold poise of Boy Harsher or Minuit Machine, but her own instinct leans more toward psychological ambiguity than brute force. She seems fascinated by the gap between what happened, what was wanted, and what gets remembered later. The best moments make uncertainty itself feel physical, a pressure in the chest that still leaves room for dancing. The accompanying video sharpens that idea by turning Sue into a modern Louise Brooks wandering through a glitch-struck universe that seems detached from ordinary chronology. Her severe bob and silent-era poise collide with digital ruptures, warped space, and fractured movement, giving the clip the look of a lost screen goddess accidentally uploaded into a corrupted future. Watch the lyric video for Details In The Dark below: Details In The Dark is out October 21, 2026 via Avant! Records. Pre-order and pre-save here. items.body: Bestial Mouths Dead Lines Negative Gain Productions Lynette Cerezo has been releasing records and performing within her Bestial Mouths project for seventeen years. Does that merit “veteran” status within the field of dark music? It’s a semantic question with no firm answer, of course, but one which comes to mind if you’ve tracked all six LPs, with new release Dead Lines coming three years after R.O.T.T. (inmyskin). By making some slight variations on Bestial Mouths’ sound, Dead Lines ironically brings the project’s strengths and larger legacy into sharper relief. At first blush, Dead Lines doesn’t stray too far from its predecessors: the always arresting and hair-raising virtuoso vocals, the musical bombast, the thematic and visual extremity are all here in spades. But if you’re halfway familiar with Bestial Mouths’ dramatic and at times violent approach to goth and darkwave sounds, cagier moves made by Cerezo and long-time collaborator Brant Showers swiftly become apparent. “Shuttered” and “Conjure” rank as some of the most accessible pieces Bestial Mouths has ever released, perhaps not so much in terms of club readiness (though savvy DJs have long been able to massage Bestial Mouths into sets), but as sweeping compositions which hit cinematic portent and Steinman-esque choral excess, respectively. While less overt than those, the well spaced and place synth strings which tiptoe through the percussive sturm und drang of “Hiss” are the sorts of details which might’ve been lost in a noisier barrage on a previous record. Flagging these moments in a record that is still as strident and bracing as Dead Lines raises the question of perspective; have changes actually occurred within Bestial Mouths, or have we longtime listeners simply better attuned ourselves to the aesthetic severity Cerezo has wielded for so long? Extremity for its own sake has never been Bestial Mouth’s remit, and there’s a clear purpose behind having martial percussion and klaxon-like vocals flood the zone on opener “Chord”. Is something as direct as an earnest AOC sample something which might have appeared on an early Bestial Mouths record? Perhaps not, but again this might be a question of perspective: that which has always been extreme perhaps seems less so in times of extremity. To again take the historical long view, Bestial Mouths have weathered a slew of scene-wide sea change since they emerged without ever allowing club trends or flash in the pan micro-genres to sway them; it’s indeed hard to detect in Dead Lines any impetus for what shifts can be found beyond the project’s own internal momentum. Cerezo, thus, is finding new ways of sounding exactly like Bestial Mouths and nothing else, even if what that means in specific changes. Recommended. Buy it. items._genre: darkwave / goth / industrial / post-punk
items._cn_summary: Bestial Mouths 第十七年的第六张全长专辑《Dead Lines》延续了乐队一贯的戏剧化、暴力美学与极端视听风格，同时在细节上展现出微妙的变化。主唱 Lynette Cerezo 标志性的高难度人声、宏大的音乐编排以及主题上的尖锐性依然是核心，但与长期合作者 Brant Showers 的合作中出现了更具可听性的走向：《Shuttered》和《Conjure》以电影化的宏大叙事和近乎史诗级的合唱编配，跻身乐队最易接受的曲目之列；《Hiss》中精心铺设的合成器弦乐在鼓击的暴风雨中若隐若现，展现出以往被噪音洪流所掩盖的层次感。乐评指出，专辑并非被动追逐俱乐部潮流或短暂亚类型，而是沿着自身内部动力推进，在极端性中寻找新的表达方式。整体而言，这是一张在继承中精进的暗潮作品，对长期听众和新入坑者都具有吸引力。

items.body: I've read other reviews of Dreadnought's upcoming release and they've described the album as more "direct". I don't know if I necessarily agree or, rather, if I think that's the main that should be highlighted. To be sure, Wars of Spirit // Wards of Light (from here on called Wars) is more direct in the sense that the more ethereal passages of previous Dreadnought releases are mostly gone. All tracks clock in under ten minutes and their structure is a bit more straight forward in how it balances the psychedelic, "lighter" elements of Dreadnought's sound and the more vociferous, black metal sound.But there's a deeper transformation for the band's sound on Wars that I think merits focus and that's a sea change in the entire palette of Dreadnought on this release. On previous releases, all the way back to Bridging Realms, Dreadnought lived on a tight rope; the band were constantly balancing those two modes I referenced above. Emergence was perhaps the exception and therefore the album which sounds the most like Wars; like it, Emergence had a more rumbling, bass-forward sound and tended to "explode" less into that other, treble and tenor focused mode of Dreadnought. Wars is very much the same, more contemplative, "richer", less prone to far flung gestures, and more dedicated to a thicker, more present sort of approach.Which is not to say it never explodes; it does. But check out the way in which it does, on opening track "Tiamat's Gate" five minute mark. In the past, this passage (the catharsis of the track) would have been accompanied by high-pitched screams, whirling float, and punctual piano. But here, the center of the weight is focused on a maelstrom like guitar riff, embellished by deep, sonorous riffs and, of course, Kelly Schilling's powerful vocals. But they are more of the "haggard" variety, with that unique timbre she has. And they trade places with a much deeper growl provided by Ryan Sims. The end result is a darker, more brooding sound. Yes, Schilling's familiar clean vocals come in later and yes, the track winds into a soaring peak. But then it's also immediately snatched into a gorgeous, muted passage punctuated by excellently restrained blast beats, darkly scintillating synths, and deep, subtle bass.This new iteration on the sound continues through the release: the synths sound fuller but also more contemplative and atmospheric for example. You can hear that on "Aeonwar", where they basically good full darkwave in their sound (beautifully melded with Schilling's gothic style). Likewise the guitars continue to be denser and thicker than before, less worried about tracing every peak and crescendo and more focused on creating texture and weight to the sound. It's on full display for "Aeonwar", with one of my favorite riffs from the band's history doing wonders "beneath" the gossamer synths. It's Dreadnought, for sure, and it's made up of the elements which first caused me to fall in love with the band. But most importantly, it champions the quality which I love Dreadnought the most for: change. Wars of Spirit // Wards of Light is a further step in the band's career, deeper into the beating, shadowed heart of their sound. Wars of Spirit // Wards of Light by Dreadnought
items._genre: black metal / darkwave / progressive / atmospheric metal
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑标志着乐队声音的深层转变。此前作品在迷幻轻盈段落与激烈黑金属之间走钢丝，如今则更倾向于厚重、低频主导的质感，爆发点减少，整体更为沉思与浓郁。吉他音墙变得更为密实，专注于创造纹理与重量而非追逐每一个高潮；合成器层次饱满却内敛，融入明显的暗潮气质，与主唱哥特风格的人声交织。低吟与粗粝咆哮交替出现，营造出更为黑暗、内省的氛围。曲目结构更为直接，少有十分钟以上的长篇，但每首歌曲在厚重riff、深沉贝斯与克制blast beat之间精心铺陈张力。这是乐队向更暗、更密、更具氛围感的迭代，融合了黑金属的攻击性与暗潮的阴郁沉思。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.
items.label: Sunnyside SCS 1813
items._genre: avant-garde jazz / vocal improvisation / experimental piano
items._cn_summary: Ran Blake与Dominique Eade合作的专辑展现了独特的选曲逻辑，将Max Roach、Mingus、Meg Whitfield Houston等风格迥异的作品并置，揭示素材之间隐秘的联系而非传统意义上的诠释。Blake的钢琴处理如同为音乐做X光扫描，暴露其内在骨骼与器官，使熟悉的作品焕发全新面貌。Eade的声乐演绎延续了Blake与女性歌手合作的核心传统，却开辟了区别于Jeanne Lee的路线——她的演唱以鲜明的喜悦感为核心特质，既能在戏剧性段落迸发情感，也能在阴郁曲目中渗透温情，逐音节雕琢歌词的能力赋予每首歌高度个人化的解读，使整张专辑既具实验性又保持极强的可亲近性。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body:
The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

Weird and wonderful, it sounds
items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是挪威Camilla Hole Trio继前作将科幻合成器音色与传统挪威民间音乐结合之后的新尝试，将目光从星际拉回地面，但探索外部音乐传统的方向未变。主奏乐器为高音萨克斯，爵士影响贯穿始终。以西挪威传统春季舞曲"Springleik"为素材的开篇曲目中，霍勒先以萨克斯呈示旋律，卡尔曼的低音提琴与内斯海姆的鼓提供节奏支撑，随后叠加模块合成器与颤音琴丰富音色。三人角色不断流动交换，卡尔曼以贝斯接续旋律并与萨克斯齐奏，内斯heim进一步拓展节奏空间，乐曲走向即兴化。整体手法显示团体刻意模糊乐器分工，以开放即兴结构重塑民间曲调，是欧洲小厂牌出品的跨领域即兴作品。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Embroiled by turbulence and tragedy, prog sludge metal masters MASTODON have pretty much ruled theroost in one of prog metal's most gritty subgenres throughout the years since the band's inceptionin 2000 having churned out four classics during their first decade run. While the 2010s may haveseen a dip in quality the band stilled sallied forth into battle delivering solid if not perfectprog sludge metal releases but then change tends to rear its ugly head in unexpected ways and shakesthings up dramatically. After 25 years founding member Brent Hinds succumbed to the tensions brewingin the band and decided to leave the band and then even more shocking died in an unfortunatemotorcycle accident soon after. Would MASTODON continue or call it a day? Given the unevenness andcontinuing decline in quality, many including myself thought it was the end. However that was notthe case. The band not only continued but returns in 2026 with its strongest album since "Crack TheSkye."MARROW DEEP is the 9th album by this Atlanta based act and a turning point in the band's history.Stepping in to fill Hinds' shoes is guitarist / vocalist Nick Johnston formerly of Osmanthus andalso added to team is keyboardist Jo�o Nogueira. A new five-piece version of MASTODON is born. Thealbum also features seven guests adding vocals, bass and percussion including Lamb of God's RandyBlythe and Black Sabbath's Geezer Butcher amongst others. Graced with yet another stylish dose ofalbum cover art that never fails to deliver, MARROW DEEP not only is a pretty album to behold butreally does bring the band full circle to the heavy sludge metal leanings that launched them intopopular favor over two decades ago. After a few wimpy albums during the last decade, the shakeupseems to have reinvigorated the band much like the latest from Neurosis and finds the band inexcellent form not only with stronger compositions but also in musical delivery. While nothing isspectacularly new in the MASTODON universe as far as stylistic approach, everything just sounds morepassionately inspired this time around.Known for their long albums, MARROW DEEP is yet another hour plus crossroads where progressivemetal, sludge metal and stoner rock converge to deliver a lethal dose of filthy sonic grit takingthe band back to the days of "Leviathan" and "Blood Mountain" which happen to be my favorite twoalbums by the band so it goes without saying that this is a much welcome reprise in the band's peakperformances of the early 2000s. The album wastes no time declaring MASTODON is back with avengeance with the opening "Barbarian's Blood" which signals the path to 65 1/2 minutes of 12 sludgytracks that deliver all the MASTODON goods in rich abundance. Steeped with dueling guitar grunge,slower contemplative moments that offer dramatic diversity and the band's uncanny progressivemeanderings, MARROW DEEP is like a big boil that popped and covering your senses with grimy oozethat absolutely reeks! You know, the way sludge metal is supposed to slap you in the face!From the bantering opener throughout there are no weak tracks on this one. Technically the last twotracks, two of my faves are the best. "The Vanishing" offers a doomy intro before erupting intofull-fueled sludgery while "The Three Fates" offers a nice jazzy keyboard break from the brashbravado and despite the presence of keys on this release, they remain fairly subdued and almostundetectable save for scant appearances where they stick out. Overall MASTODON threw the ultimatecurveball in 2026 with MARROW DEEP and along with Neurosis proved that old dogs can still learn newtricks although nothing's really substantially new on this release but rather picking up in a waywhere "Crack The Skye" left off and adding the quality control back to the entire album's playingtime. While i wouldn't call this the band's absolute best, i would call it the best since theirfirst four releases. A stellar year for MASTODON fans it is!

items._cn_summary: Mastodon 在创始成员 Brent Hinds 离队并意外去世后重新集结，形成五人编制并加入新吉他手与键盘手，于2026年推出第九张专辑。乐评认为这是乐队自《Crack The Skye》以来最强的一次回归，方向重回早期《Leviathan》与《Blood Mountain》的泥泞金属质感。全碟12首歌时长约65分钟，开篇曲即宣告强硬姿态，作品在厚重失真、双吉他交织、慢板营造与前卫变奏之间切换，整体偏向污泥金属与石人摇滚的混合体，兼具粗粝的噪音美学和复杂的叙事结构。多名客座乐手参与为专辑增添层次。乐评指出风格上没有明显突破，但执行力与情感浓度明显提升，较前十年几张偏弱的专辑更具说服力。对于偏好实验声响与非主流美学的听众而言，该作仍属于金属框架内的回归之作，而非跨界实验。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It was a strange era, a time of change and readjustment, and one where it was easy to lose one's way. Musicians who wished to stay the course had to confront record labels and even critics who accused them of self-plagiarism; yet, on the other hand, changing direction was seen as an act of betrayal. Nevertheless, Jon Anderson transitioned from making his recording debut as a solo artist to surrounding himself with friends for his second album, Song of Seven, a number that held deep significance for him, symbolizing both the inner quest and a sense of wholeness.The lineup included Dick Morrissey, saxophonist for the jazz-fusion band If; bassist John Giblin (formerly of Brand X); and Morris Pert on drums and percussion, along with, of course, Jack Bruce and Simon Phillips. With this dynamic, groove-laden band, plus additional musicians and a string quartet, Jon handled acoustic guitar, keyboards, and the harp. He composed songs that, while initially striking due to their ultra-modern, early-80s production style (as heard on "For You for Me"), ultimately reveal themselves to be classic Anderson tracks: deeply emotional and reminiscent of his collaborations with Vangelis. It is an epic sound; backed by such solid musicians, the music creates a rich sonic tapestry that colors the scene much like the stained-glass artwork on the album cover. "Some Are Born" is a beautiful acoustic song that could easily have fit into the Yes repertoire had he been recording with his bandmates.There are symphonic touches alongside rhythms that were more contemporary for that era, such as soul, funk, and a bit of jazz (though not the most daring kind). There is something ethnic about "Don't Forget (Nostalgia), something Latin, that is enhanced by John Dankworth's saxophone; meanwhile, "Heart of the Matter," despite its more pop-rock format, is filled with Jon's signature positive energy, and the rhythm section of Jack Bruce on bass and Simon Phillips on drums provides excellent support for the track."Hear It" is a beautiful track, one could easily imagine it within the context of Yes, yet it stands on its own; it embodies Jon's spirit, which possesses a distinct identity of its own, always positive and visionary, inviting the listener to share in that outlook. "Everybody Loves You" has a rhythm that always reminded me of the songs Carole King and Gerry Goffin used to write; I could even picture it on Tapestry. The bass work, along with Morris Pert's percussion, lends the track a warm, jazzy feel, while the arrangement retains a certain complexity toward the end."Take Your Time" is almost a beautiful waltz, enhanced by Giblin's fretless bass and unmistakably Anderson-esque. By the time "Days" arrives, the album has transcended any specific era to become timeless; it features Jon, his guitar, and his signature magic, with minimal keyboard and bass accompaniment, just enough to let the music of his words cast the spell."Song of Seven" is, logically, the title track, and for me, it acts as a counterweight to the rest of the 'lbum, working not in isolation, but as part of the whole. The strings usher in a different atmosphere, one that is more sacred, and mark the point of greatest resemblance to Yes; indeed, at times it is hard to distinguish it from that band, given Jon's unmistakable voice. Rich in melody and character, the song stands tall on its own merits, earning a place among the very best in his repertoire, akin in spirit to the Going for the One era of Yes.A solid album that fits perfectly into the discography and perfectly explains the subsequent trajectory, including further adventures with Vangelis on Short Stories (1980) and Animation (1982), thereby rounding out that concept of wholeness.
items._genre: progressive rock / art rock / pop rock / jazz-funk
items._cn_summary: Jon Anderson 的第二张个人专辑组建了包含 Jack Bruce、Simon Phillips 等乐手的融合乐队，并加入弦乐四重奏，以 80 年代初的现代制作风格呈现其标志性旋律。歌曲在抒情摇滚基底上融入灵魂、放克、爵士与拉丁节奏，既有接近 Yes 气质的段落，也有民谣式和华尔兹式作品。整张专辑贯穿着 Anderson 积极、富有远见的精神，管乐与节奏组交织出丰富的声响层次，乐评认为它超越了具体时代，成为典型的 Anderson 式创作。

items.body: Margate, Kent-based musician Tim Horne has released “An Ocean Apart”, the first single from his new album “Transmutation”, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts. Horne composes cinematic ambient and electronic music using synthesisers, acoustic instruments and field recordings. “An Ocean Apart” comes with a video by @diz_qo, built around artwork by Mariz Nigro, and the single is also available on Spotify and Apple Music. Horne describes “An Ocean Apart” as the emotional core of the album. “It forms the emotional core of the album and is imbued with paradoxical feelings of distance and closeness, isolation and connection. These are contradictory emotions I’ve oscillated between when looking back with unreliable memory and nostalgia,” he said. Tim Horne’s ‘Transmutation’ due October 8 “Transmutation” runs eight tracks: “Requiem,” “Halcyon,” “Biota,” “An Ocean Apart,” “Volta,” “Folie à Deux,” “Ascension” and “Metamorphosis.” Horne wrote, performed and produced every track himself, with additional mixing and mastering by Thomas Farmer and artwork by Mariz Nigro. The album was recorded towards the end of a long-term relationship and works through contradictory memories of joy and sorrow alongside an embrace of change. Horne layers flute and other acoustic instruments with analog, digital and modular synthesizers, often processing them until they no longer resemble their source material. He has pointed to Wendy Carlos, Kraftwerk, Boards of Canada, Sigur Rós, M83, Radiohead, Nils Frahm, Alessandro Cortini, R Beny, Emily Sprague, Ann Annie, Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, Jogging House and Hainbach as influences on the record. Transmutation by Tim Horne “Transmutation” is available to pre-order now as a digital album and as a limited-edition CD in a card wallet, both through Bandcamp, with the full record following on release day. About Tim Horne Tim Horne is a musician based in Margate, Kent. He spent roughly a decade playing bass, synthesisers and backing vocals in bands including Linear Loveboxx, Inca Maps and Inigo Blue & The System before moving into solo work. He self-released two solo albums built from modular-synthesizer improvisation, “Rise” (2022) and “Clusters” (2023). Horne developed his current sound over two years through the regular live sessions hosted by Coastal Electronauts, a collective of electronic and experimental artists based in nearby Whitstable, and that process led to the eight tracks on “Transmutation.” The album, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts, follows those two solo releases and is preceded by the single “An Ocean Apart.”
items._genre: ambient / electronic / experimental / cinematic
items._cn_summary: Tim Horne 来自肯特郡马尔盖特，新专辑《Transmutation》由他独自撰写、演奏并制作，混音与母带交由 Thomas Farmer 完成。作品以模拟、数字与模块合成器叠加长笛等原声乐器，并融入田野录音，常将声源处理至难以辨认原始形态，体现实验性的声音设计理念。专辑创作于一段长期感情的尾声，探讨记忆的不可靠与怀旧情绪中喜悦与哀伤的矛盾交织。首支单曲《An Ocean Apart》被 Horne 描述为整张专辑的情感核心，呈现疏离与亲近、孤独与连结的悖论。专辑共八首曲目，时长与发行形式涵盖数字与限量 CD 版本。他此前的两张个人专辑均以模块合成器即兴为基础，本作则经过约两年的现场打磨逐步成型。

items.body: Review by SeeHatfield — I know next to nothing about the history of PFM (apart from what I've read here on Prog Archives and on Wikipedia), and I couldn't name the band's members without referencing a cheat sheet. I usually don't have any idea of what they're singing about, either. But I've been listening to them on and off for the better part of forty years, and I know their first five studio albums (plus the English-language adaptations of two of them). I thank a prog-loving friend for making me a tape of Storia Di Un Minuto and its follow-up, Per Un Amico, back in my undergrad days; those two albums in particular cast a spell on me.Without ever researching the lyrics or the band, I came to love those two records (even as I somehow lost or ditched my copy of the English-language Photos of Ghosts along the way). I've come to realize that I greatly prefer the very early PFM, when it included flautist and violinist Mauro Pagani and did not yet include vocalist Bernardo Lanzetti. I think those were the prime years.Storia Di Un Minuto must surely count as one of the great debuts in progressive rock. It's tuneful, inventive, dynamic, and fun, channeling obvious Crimso and Tull influences in the direction of richly melodic, romantic Italianicity. It's eminently hummable, an album of great themes and fragments, with so many moments that stick in my mind. I won't go into detail, but must note that this is exactly what I like about vintage prog: the feeling of several musicians putting their heads and hands together and treating the studio like a laboratory. There's a lot of skill in these five players, but more important than their chops is their enthusiasm for raiding the rag basket, stitching together so many disparate elements, and pushing themselves past their limits. There's a shamelessness about this kind of music, and a sheer love of discovery. Storia Di Un Minuto, at just under 35 minutes, is so full of good stuff that it's a bit of a miracle."Impressioni di Settembre," with its upward-straining melodic hook at the end of each verse (that lovely upsurge of mellotron and Moog), is PFM's "Crimson King," while "La Carrozza di Hans" weds Tullish flute to a frantic, "Schizoid Man"-style 6/8 section and, "Aqualung"-style, jams together different bits into a frantic musical puzzle. These moves are familiar, but with PFM the delight is the distinctiveness of their own melodies. Also, the singing, though divvied up among several members, is good throughout (I've never thought of Lanzetti as an improvement). In a few years, PFM would crank up the heavy rock, bank on their skill, and lose some of their early delicacy (listen to the virtuosic hammering of Chocolate Kings to know what I mean). I think that's too bad. The good stuff was the exploratory early stuff, which happened to birth some excellent songs and lovely scraps. Maybe I should figure out the lyrics now?

items.body: Liars will release their new album A Ban On Plastic Bag Bans through Mute Records on 5 March 2027. The band, now the solo recording vehicle of Angus Andrew, has shared the first single, “Ice Pick, Kalamazoo,” alongside UK and European tour dates in October. “Ice Pick, Kalamazoo” takes its title from the city in Michigan where Andrew relocated with his wife and daughter. Soon after moving, he noticed a persistent smell around the family home and his daughter’s school, traced to hydrogen sulphide and other pollutants released by a local packaging factory at levels the state health department flagged as dangerous enough to advise residents to stay indoors. Andrew got involved in a campaign to hold the factory accountable, and the experience, and its tangle of environmental damage, corporate responsibility and bureaucratic inertia, became the starting point for the new album. “A Ban On Plastic Bag Bans” takes its title from an actual Michigan statute that bars local governments from banning single-use plastic bags, a piece of legislation Andrew found emblematic of how attempts to reduce environmental harm can themselves become targets for prohibition. “You become so used to something, you lose your sense of it,” Andrew said of the theme running through the record: how injustice settles into the background of daily life, and how draining it becomes to keep pushing against institutions built to outlast that resistance. The album was written and recorded across the United States and Australia, where Andrew now lives, in collaboration with drummer Laurence Pike and multi-instrumentalist Cameron Deyell, both of whom worked on 2021’s “The Apple Drop” and have toured with Liars since 2017’s “TFCF”. Rather than building the songs from finished demos, the three musicians worked through improvisation, developing material across continents by ear rather than by score. Andrew describes the result as a different kind of political record, one concerned less with protest itself than with the toll of sustaining it. “It wasn’t just the environment that was polluted,” he said. “It was also my mind.” “A Ban On Plastic Bag Bans” will be released on white recycled and recyclable PET vinyl, CD and digital formats. The tracklist runs: “Happy Or Not,” “Ice Pick, Kalamazoo,” “Laced Plume,” “Urgent As Always,” “Deep Deeper,” “Disaster Tropes,” “Beat Creep Some Eyes,” “Real Time Trespasser,” “SHAME!,” “Retention Arc” and “Out Of Order.” The period leading up to the album followed the disruption of the pandemic, when touring plans for “The Apple Drop” fell through and Andrew stepped back from making new Liars music for the first time since his teens. He spent the time on other projects instead, founding the record label No Gold and the experimental platform Essential Tremors. “Both of those things were really about listening,” he said, describing the shift away from being “a full-time creator” toward closer engagement with other artists and with his adopted surroundings in Kalamazoo. Liars tour dates for ‘A Ban On Plastic Bag Bans’ The album announcement comes with UK and European tour dates, giving audiences a rare chance to see the band’s live show in intimate rooms, plus a one-off 20th-anniversary performance of “Drums Not Dead” with two Polish percussionists, including Macio Moretti, at Unsound Festival. Tickets go on sale from 10am local time on 11 September via the band’s official site. 2 October – Bucharest, Romania – Control Club (Opening Party) 3 October – Nantes, France – Le Lieu Unique 5 October – Milan, Italy – Arci Bellezza 9 October – Krakow, Poland – Unsound Festival (“Drums Not Dead” 20th-anniversary performance) 10 October – Belgrade, Serbia – Changeover Festival 12 October – Prague, Czech Republic – Punctum 13 October – Berlin, Germany – Neue Zukunft 15 October – Amsterdam, Netherlands – Paradiso 17 October – Kortrijk, Belgium – Atelier Nooitgedacht 18 October – Liege, Belgium – Kultura 20 October – London, UK – Moth Club 22 October – Paris, France – Boule Noire 24 October – Copenhagen, Denmark – Ideal Bar About Liars Angus Andrew and Aaron Hemphill met in the late 1990s in Los Angeles, where Andrew was studying photography at CalArts and Hemphill worked at a local record store. The two began recording together before relocating to New York, where they answered a musicians’ wanted ad from bassist Pat Noecker and drummer Ron Albertson. The four-piece was formally christened Liars in New York in November 2000. Working with producer Steve Revitte, the band recorded its debut album, “They Threw Us All in a Trench and Stuck a Monument on Top,” in two days; it was released in October 2001 on Gern Blandsten Records, with Blast First and later Mute Records handling subsequent reissues. Albertson left the band in 2000 before the debut’s release, and Noecker departed in 2002; multi-instrumentalist Julian Gross joined in 2003. Liars moved to Mute Records for 2004’s “They Were Wrong, So We Drowned” and continued releasing albums on the label through 2006’s “Drums Not Dead,” their self-titled 2007 album, 2010’s “Sisterworld,” 2012’s “WIXIW,” 2014’s “Mess,” 2017’s “TFCF” and 2021’s “The Apple Drop.” Hemphill left the band amicably around the release of “TFCF,” after which Andrew continued Liars as a solo recording project, working with a rotating cast of collaborators including Laurence Pike and Cameron Deyell. Since “The Apple Drop,” Andrew has also run the label No Gold and the experimental platform Essential Tremors from Australia, where he now lives. “A Ban On Plastic Bag Bans,” due 5 March 2027 on Mute, is Liars’ tenth studio album and their first release since “The Apple Drop,” accompanied by their first UK and European live dates in years.

items._cn_summary: Liars 新专辑《A Ban On Plastic Bag Bans》由 Angus Andrew 作为个人创作载体，跨越美国与澳大利亚两地，与鼓手 Laurence Pike 及多乐器演奏者 Cameron Deyell 通过远程即兴方式完成录制，摒弃成品 demo，以听觉协作构建曲目结构。专辑灵感源自 Andrew 移居密歇根州卡拉马祖后遭遇的工厂污染事件，以及当地禁止地方政府禁用塑料袋的法规，由此延伸至制度性不公如何沉淀为日常背景、持续抵抗所带来的精神消耗这一核心主题。Andrew 自陈这张专辑并非传统抗议唱片，而是聚焦于抗议本身的代价——污染的不仅是环境，也是心智。专辑将以再生 PET 白胶唱片、CD 及数字格式发行。整体属于独立实验摇滚范畴，带有工业与后朋克的底色，即兴创作方式为其增添了一层实验色彩。
